By what certain argument of faith can you prove the approving popes were lawful and did not seize the see by force or simony? At best you have historical and moral certainty, which does not suffice for faith.

How will anyone trust that copies of councils and papal decrees are uncorrupted, with nothing added or cut, when it is certain many decrees were fastened on popes and many councils' acts corrupted and spoiled?
A fresh papal or conciliar declaration will not end the doubt: the same difficulties rise against the latest council as against the earlier one, and so without end.
If their case against Scripture's certainty and authority stands, the authority of church, councils, and popes falls with it — and no foundation of faith is left.

source_text: XIX. Imo ausim dicere ne quidem animo fingi posse ullum fidei fundamentum adversus quod non liceat similibus uti cavillationibus. Quicquid enim proferetur tanquam prima fidei regula, necesse est ut sit aliquid logice inevidens, & quod non possit proprie demonstrari. Nam principia fidei, ex communi Theologorum & Scholasticorum consensu, sunt inevidentia & indemonstrabilia. Ac praeterea necesse est ut non possit ex aliis fidei principiis tanquam prioribus & notioribus probari, alioqui prima regula non esset, sed daretur aliqua prior. Unde necessario sequitur primam fidei regulam, cujus authoritas quoad nos suprema est, esse aliquid quod argumentis de fide a priori probari non possit, & super quo etiam non possit satisfieri profanorum hominum quaestionibus per demonstrationes, & rationes prorsus necessarias atque evidentes.
english: I dare say one cannot even imagine a foundation of faith against which the same cavils would not be lawful.

Whatever is offered as faith's first rule must be something logically inevident and not properly demonstrable. Theologians and scholastics agree: the principles of faith are inevident and indemonstrable.
Nor can it be proved from other, prior, better-known principles of faith — or it would not be first, and some earlier rule would take its place.

So the first rule of faith, whose authority for us is supreme, cannot be proved by arguments of faith a priori, nor can the questions of irreligious men be met about it by demonstrations and strictly necessary, evident reasons.

source_text: XX. Sed ut istius sophismatis vanitas clarius appareat, notandum in eo multa praesupponi quae omnino falsa sunt. Et primo quidem supponit illud omne nobis esse dubium & incertum quod a multis negatur, & de quo sunt multi qui dubitant. At si hoc admittatur nihil prorsus certum remanebit. Vix enim quicquam est tam certum & evidens, de quo non fuerit a multis dubitatum; imo quod a multis negatum non fuerit. Ita nobis certum non erit ex caeli & terrae aspectu Deum esse, quoniam Epicurei & Athei hoc negant. Neque prima principia scientiarum nobis certa erunt, & indubitata, quoniam Pyrrhonii, qui assensum omnem tollebant, de istis quoque dubitarunt. Neque Pontificiis, ut diximus, certa erit Ecclesiae suae authoritas, quoniam a reliquis Christianis negatur. Itaque dicendum id de quo immerito dubitatur, & quod sine ratione negatur, non desinere certum esse recte sentientibus. Nec enim hominum male feriatorum, perversorum atque stultorum error & dubitatio circa res in se certas, quicquam obest certitudini hominum sani judicii, & quorum mens recte affecta est.
english: To see the sophism's emptiness more clearly, note how many false things it assumes.

First it assumes that whatever many deny, or many doubt, is doubtful and uncertain for us. Admit that, and nothing certain remains. Almost nothing so certain and evident has escaped doubt — or flat denial — from many.

Then it would not be certain from the sight of heaven and earth that God is, because Epicureans and atheists deny it. First principles of the sciences would not be certain, because Pyrrhonians who suspended all assent doubted them too. And Rome's own church authority would not be certain for Romanists, because the rest of Christians deny it.

What is doubted without desert, and denied without reason, does not cease to be certain for those who judge rightly. The error and doubt of idle, perverse, foolish people about things certain in themselves do not touch the certainty of sound minds rightly disposed.

source_text: XXI. Deinde supponitur in isto argumento id quod demonstrari non potest, & necessariis ac evidentibus argumentis probari, non posse esse fidei certum & exploratum, certamque apud fideles fidei regulam atque fundamentum. At hoc est falsissimum. Etenim prima fidei regula, quaecunque tandem statuatur, necesse omnino est ut sit aliquid, quod evidentibus, &, si logice loquamur, prorsus necessariis argumentis probari non potest. Siquidem argumenta illa, vel ex proprio ipsius testimonio peterentur, vel ex aliis fidei principiis, vel ex humana ratione. Jam vero peti non possunt ex ipsius testimonio, quoniam hoc modo nihil probat seipsum: non etiam ex aliis fidei principiis, quia quod ponitur esse prima fidei regula hoc ipso supponitur esse principium fidei notissimum, ad quod proinde probandum, alia minus nota frustra adhiberentur; nisi forte ad hominem: denique non ex humana ratione; quia, cum regula fidei sit aliquid proprie loquendo inevidens, non potest rationibus necessariis demonstrari, sed solum argumentis moralibus suaderi.
english: Next the argument assumes that what cannot be demonstrated by necessary and evident proofs cannot be certain for faith, or a sure rule and foundation of faith among believers. That is utterly false.
Whatever first rule of faith you set must be something that cannot be proved by evident — and, speaking logically, strictly necessary — arguments.

Such proofs would have to come from its own testimony, from other principles of faith, or from human reason. It cannot prove itself from its own witness. It cannot be proved from other faith-principles, because as first rule it is already supposed the best-known principle — so weaker ones would be useless except perhaps ad hominem. And it cannot be proved from human reason: a rule of faith is properly inevident, and so can only be urged by moral arguments, not demonstrated by necessary ones.

source_text: XXII. Tertio, istud argumentum supponit dubitationes illas quas adversus Scripturam movere potest humana ratio per Ecclesiae authoritatem tolli. Sed hoc quoque falsum est. Nam quaerenti unde scimus libros qui circumferuntur Apostolorum & Prophetarum esse, aut omnino fuisse Apostolos & Prophetas ullos, non satis fit dicendo Ecclesiam ita dicere & docere. Siquidem pari jure quaeret ille unde scimus Ecclesiam verum dicere, & duci a Spiritu sancto. At cum tot sint sectae inter Christianos, unde scimus hanc potius quam illam esse veram Ecclesiam, aut ullam omnino esse in terris Dei Ecclesiam. Certe tum ipsis nihil supererit quo se adversus ejusmodi percunctatorem tueantur, nisi notae & praejudicia illa quibus Ecclesiae Romanae authoritas ipsorum judicio redditur credibilis. Verum hic non quaeruntur ejusmodi argumenta, sed quae certo probent rem esse de fide, & quibus fides tanquam suo fundamento niti possit. Ac praeterea, si istuc deveniendum foret, promptum est nobis ostendere Scripturae authoritatem longe pluribus & certioribus argumentis & notis commendari, quam cujuscunque inter Christianos Ecclesiae authoritatem.
english: Third, the argument assumes that doubts human reason can raise against Scripture are cleared by the Church's authority. That too is false.

To someone asking how we know circulating books are the Apostles' and Prophets', or that there ever were Apostles and Prophets, it is not enough to say the Church so teaches — he will ask with equal right how we know the Church speaks truth and is led by the Spirit.

With so many Christian sects, how do we know this rather than that is the true Church — or that any Church of God is on earth at all? Then they have nothing left against such an inquirer but those marks and prejudices that make Rome's authority look credible to them.

But what we need here is not that kind of probability — it is what proves the matter to be of faith and can bear faith as its foundation. And if we did have to go there, we are ready to show that Scripture's authority is recommended by far more and surer arguments and marks than any Christian church's.

source_text: XXIII. Sed, ut jam pressius agamus, ista sunt ad argumentum propositum applicanda. Argumentum fuit ejusmodi. Quod ex se nobis est dubium & incertum firma fide a nobis apprehendi non potest, nisi authoritate aliqua superiori confirmetur. Sed Scriptura ex se nobis dubia & incerta est. Ergo necesse est eam authoritate aliqua superiori confirmari. Quae alia esse non potest quam Ecclesiae authoritas. Respondeo aliquid nobis dubium & incertum dici potest duplici respectu. Nempe fidei respectu: deinde respectu rationis humanae. Fidei incertum est quod a Deo revelatum & inspiratum non est. At rationi humanae incertum est quod demonstrari non potest argumentis necessariis & evidentibus. Itaque distinguenda minor, Scriptura ex se nobis dubia & incerta. Nam, si illud nobis dicatur, respectu rationis humanae concedi potest, si vero respectu fidei neganda est. Quamvis enim Scriptura rationi etiam humanae suaderi & commendari possit multis bonis & validis argumentis: Attamen quia ista argumenta logice & mathematice demonstrativa non sunt, eatenus patimur Scripturam dici humanae rationi incertam. Sed falsum est fidei non posse esse certum quod rationi incertum est, nec demonstrari potest. Imo quod demonstrari potest eatenus res fidei non est.
english: But to deal more closely now, apply this to the argument on the table. It runs like this: what is doubtful and uncertain to us of itself cannot be firmly believed unless some higher authority confirms it; Scripture of itself is doubtful and uncertain to us; therefore some higher authority must confirm it — and that can only be the Church.
I answer that something can be called doubtful and uncertain to us in two respects: with respect to faith, and with respect to human reason.

Uncertain for faith is what God has not revealed and inspired. Uncertain for human reason is what cannot be shown by necessary and evident proofs. So distinguish the minor: Scripture of itself is doubtful and uncertain to us. Said of human reason, that can be granted; said of faith, it must be denied.

Scripture can of course be urged on human reason with many good, weighty arguments. Because those arguments are not logical or mathematical demonstrations, we allow that Scripture may be called uncertain to human reason. But it is false that what reason finds uncertain and indemonstrable cannot be certain for faith. What can be demonstrated is, to that extent, not a matter of faith at all.

source_text: XXIV. Ad majorem vero illam, Quod ex se nobis est dubium & incertum firma fide non potest apprehendi, & esse certa fidei regula, nisi authoritate superiore confirmetur. Resp. falsissimam esse, si per illud quod nobis est incertum intelligatur id quod demonstrari non potest, & argumentis prorsus necessariis confirmari. Etenim quod probari non potest argumentis, philosophice & proprie loquendo, necessariis & evidentibus, firma tamen fide potest apprehendi, & esse certa fidei regula, quamvis authoritate quoad nos superiori & priori non confirmetur. Imo, ut jamjam probavimus, omnino necesse est ut prima fidei regula sit aliquid inevidens, quod demonstrari non possit, nec tamen superiori authoritate confirmari aut queat aut debeat. Quandoquidem hoc pacto non esset, ut supponitur, prima & suprema fidei regula, sed subalterna tantum & inferior.
english: As for the major — that what is doubtful and uncertain to us of itself cannot be firmly grasped or stand as a sure rule of faith unless a higher authority confirms it — the reply is that this is utterly false if "uncertain to us" means "what cannot be demonstrated and confirmed by wholly necessary arguments."

What cannot be proved by necessary and evident arguments in the philosophical sense can still be firmly believed and be a sure rule of faith, even without confirmation from an authority prior and superior for us.

As we have just shown, the first rule of faith must be something non-evident that cannot be demonstrated — and that neither can nor should be confirmed by a higher authority. Otherwise it would not be, as supposed, faith's first and supreme rule, but only a subordinate, inferior one.

source_text: XXV. Ad minoris vero confirmationem, qua probatum est Scripturae sacrae libros esse dubios citra Ecclesiae authoritatem, quoniam multi libri Apostolis suppositi sunt, & de veris eorum scriptis dubitatum est. Resp. quod dubium est hominibus ignaris, perversis, aut non satis instructis, posse tamen esse certum fidelibus & piis, qui abunde instructi sunt, & a Spiritu sancto illuminati. Nec enim temeraria & injusta quorundam dubitatio quicquam obest certitudini hominum sani judicii.
english: As for the confirmation of the minor — that Scripture's books are doubtful apart from the Church because many books were foisted on the Apostles and genuine writings were doubted — the reply is that what is doubtful to the ignorant, the perverse, or the poorly taught can still be certain for the faithful and devout who are well taught and enlightened by the Holy Spirit.
Rash, unjust doubt from some people does nothing to shake the certainty of those with sound judgment.

source_text: XXVI. Quod autem spectat importunas illas interrogationes, Unde probatis Apostolos fuisse & scripsisse libros instinctu divino, & eos qui circumferuntur revera illorum esse? Resp. a nobis aliquid injustum exigi, nempe ut demonstremus quod est indemonstrabile. Itaque fatemur ultro ista non posse a nobis demonstrari, & mathematice seu logice probari. Sed inde negamus sequi libros istos esse non posse certam & primam fidei regulam; quoniam hoc proprium est principiis fidei ut sint inevidentia, neque probari possint argumentis philosophice necessariis & evidentibus. Quae tamen ita accipienda non sunt, ut jam saepe observatum est, quasi nihil habeamus quod hominibus profanis regerere possimus, & impiis eorum quaestionibus opponere. Nobis enim non desunt argumenta quae viro prudenti satis esse possint, & ipsi suadere Apostolos & Prophetas instinctu divino scripsisse, & nos in manibus habere genuinos eorum libros: cujus generis argumenta multa harum thesium parte prima, proposuimus & explicuimus, nec opus est hic illa repetere. Hoc solum fatemur argumenta illa non habere evidentiam logicam, seu mathematicam, & eatenus rem relinquere incertam, si libet incertum vocare quod est inevidens, & ἀναπόδεικτον. Sed hoc quoque addimus, si quid incertitudinis argumenta illa relinquunt, minime tolli posse per Ecclesiae quoddam judicium & determinationem, ut jamjam probatum est.
english: As for those importunate questions — How do you prove the Apostles existed and wrote by divine impulse, and that the circulating books are truly theirs? — something unjust is being demanded of us: that we demonstrate what is indemonstrable.

We freely admit that we cannot demonstrate those things mathematically or logically. We deny that it follows that those books cannot be faith's certain first rule. It belongs to faith's principles to be non-evident and not provable by philosophically necessary and evident arguments.

That does not mean we have nothing to answer profane objectors. We have arguments enough for a prudent person — that the Apostles and Prophets wrote by divine impulse, and that we hold their genuine books — many of which we already set out in Part I of these theses; there is no need to repeat them here.

We only grant that those arguments lack logical or mathematical evidence, and so leave the matter "uncertain" if one chooses to call the non-evident and undemonstrable (anapodeikton) uncertain. Even so, whatever uncertainty they leave cannot be cleared by some church judgment or determination — as we have just proved.

source_text: XXVII. Atque haec de isto argumento jam satis. Pergendum ad aliud. Igitur Pontificii Scripturae authoritatem quoad nos ab authoritate Ecclesiae pendere, probare quoque student ex usu & praxi Ecclesiae. Nam, inquiunt, quod libri Apocryphi, quos impostores varii sub nomine Prophetarum & Apostolorum ediderunt, & tanquam sacros & divinos obtrudere conati sunt, a fidelibus rejecti fuerunt & explosi, factum est authoritate & judicio Ecclesiae, quae libros illos supposititios, pro sua sapientia, a divinis discrevit, & e Canone expunxit: aut saltem nunquam judicavit esse recipiendos. Atque in hanc rem afferunt ex Patribus multa testimonia. Ut quod autor synopseos quae tribuitur Athanasio, rationem afferens quare Evangelia illa Thomae, Petri, secundum Hebraeos, &c. non approbentur, Quatuor, inquit, nobis Evangeliorum libros sacri sanctae Catholicae Ecclesiae Canones sanxerunt, praeter istos non est tutum aliud. Et similiter Augustinus Evangelium quoddam Thomae, quod Manichaei proferebant, repudiat his verbis, Huic Scripturae licet nobis non credere, quia non est in Catholico Canone; Et iterum, Has Scripturas Canon Ecclesiasticus respuit. Quibus addunt Eusebium, qui in historia Ecclesiastica, saepe scripta istiusmodi Apocrypha esse pronunciat, quia apud veteres nulla sit eorum mentio. Et quia nullus Scriptor Ecclesiasticus usus est testimoniis ex libris illis depromptis: aut usquam in scriptis suis in memoriam illa redigere dignatus est.
english: Enough on that argument. On to another. The Roman doctors also try to prove that Scripture's authority for us hangs on the Church's from the Church's use and practice.

Apocryphal books, they say, which impostors published under Prophets' and Apostles' names and tried to pass off as sacred, were rejected and exploded by the faithful — and that was by the Church's authority and judgment, which wisely separated those forgeries from the divine books and struck them from the Canon, or at least never judged them receivable.

They pile up Fathers for this. The synopsis attributed to Athanasius, explaining why the Gospels of Thomas, Peter, according to the Hebrews, and the like are not approved, says the Canons of the holy Catholic Church sanctioned four Gospel books for us; besides those it is not safe to have another.

Augustine likewise rejects a Gospel of Thomas the Manichees were offering: We need not believe this Scripture, because it is not in the Catholic Canon; and again, The ecclesiastical Canon rejects these Scriptures. They add Eusebius, who in the Ecclesiastical History often calls such writings Apocrypha because the ancients never mention them, and no church writer cites them or bothers to record them.

source_text: XXVIII. Cum vero de quibusdam libris vere divinis & Apostolicis aliquando inter ipsos orthodoxos dubitatum sit, ut ex. gr. de Epistola ad Hebraeos, de Epistola Jacobi, de Epistola Judae, & posteriore Epistola Petri, & de secunda & tertia Joannis, ejusdemque Apocalypsi, id inde factum afferunt & pertendunt, quod Ecclesia de his libris judicium & sententiam suam nondum pronunciarat: istam vero dubitationem tandem per Ecclesiae determinationem & judicium sublatam fuisse. Nempe in Laodicena Synodo, & III. Carthaginiensi, Innocentiiique & Gelasii PP. decretis, quibus non tantum praedicti Novi Testamenti libri, sed illi quoque de quibus adhuc hodie lis est inter nos & Pontificios, An ad Veteris Testamenti Canonem pertineant, in Scripturae Canonem, ut quidem illi volunt, recepti sunt. Atque in hujus rei confirmationem afferunt etiam quod de Epistola Jacobi scribit Hieronymus, Et si ab alio quodam sub ejus nomine scripta afferebatur, tamen paulatim procedente tempore obtinuit authoritatem. Et quod de Epistola Judae similiter dicit, Quod, etsi a plerisque rejiciebatur, tamen authoritatem vetustate & usu meruit. Quibus consentanea sunt quae de Epistola quoque ad Hebraeos, & Joannis Apocalypsi scribit idem Hieronymus epistola ad Dardanum, Nos, inquit, utraque recipimus, nequaquam hujus temporis consuetudinem, sed, veterum Scriptorum authoritatem sequentes, qui plerumque utriusque utuntur testimoniis, non ut interdum de Apocryphis facere solent, sed quasi Canonicis & Ecclesiasticis.
english: When even among the orthodox some truly divine and Apostolic books were sometimes doubted — Hebrews, James, Jude, 2 Peter, 2–3 John, and the Apocalypse — they claim this was because the Church had not yet given its judgment, and that the doubt was finally lifted by church determination: at Laodicea, the third council of Carthage, and the decrees of Popes Innocent and Gelasius.
By those, they say, not only the New Testament books just named, but also the Old Testament books still disputed between us and Rome, were received into the Canon — as they would have it.

For confirmation they cite Jerome on James: though it was being put about as written by someone else under his name, little by little it gained authority. On Jude: though most rejected it, antiquity and use earned it authority.

In the same vein Jerome writes to Dardanus on Hebrews and John's Apocalypse: We receive both, following not present custom but the authority of the ancient writers, who usually cite both not as they sometimes do the Apocrypha, but as Canonical and Ecclesiastical.

source_text: XXIX. Denique, cum multi libri quorum authoritas semper certa fuit apud Orthodoxos, ab haereticis rejecti aut in dubium vocati sint, in eo multi sunt Pontificii, ut ostendant Patres refellisse illos haereticos ex authoritate, consensu, & testimonio Ecclesiae, quibus librorum istorum divinitatem & authoritatem vindicarunt & asseruerunt. Ita enim ex. gr. Augustinus loquitur de Actis Apostolorum, quorum authoritatem Manichaei negabant, Huic libro necesse est me credere, si credo Evangelio: cum utramque Scripturam pariter nobis Catholica commendet authoritas. Et adversus eosdem Manichaeos, Nostrorum, inquit, librorum authoritas tot gentium confessione, per successiones Apostolorum, Episcoporum, Conciliorumque roborata, vobis adversa est: Vestrorum autem nulla est, quae a tam paucis profertur, &c. Ex quibus & similibus concludunt Pontificii fidem nostram de Scriptura sacra ab Ecclesiae judicio pendere: ejusque authoritatem, testimonium & consensum esse regulam & amussim, ad quam Scriptura omnis probanda & examinanda est, ut certo de ea nobis constare possit: juxta celebre illud Augustini, Ego vero Evangelio non crederem nisi me Catholicae Ecclesiae commoveret authoritas. Et quod alibi dicit idem vir sanctus. Tenebit hunc modum fidelis animus in Scripturis Canonicis, ut eas quae ab omnibus accipiuntur Ecclesiis Catholicis praeponat eis quas quaedam non accipiunt. De iis vero quae non accipiuntur ab omnibus, praeferet eas quas plures gravioresque accipiunt, eis quas pauciores minorisque authoritatis Ecclesiae tenent.
english: Finally, when heretics rejected or doubted many books whose authority was always sure among the Orthodox, many Roman doctors try to show that the Fathers refuted them from the Church's authority, consent, and testimony, by which they vindicated those books' divinity and authority.

So Augustine on Acts, which the Manichees denied: I must believe this book if I believe the Gospel, since Catholic authority recommends both Scriptures to us alike. And against the same: The authority of our books, strengthened by so many nations' confession through the successions of Apostles, bishops, and councils, stands against you; yours has none, being put forward by so few.

From this and the like they conclude that our faith about sacred Scripture hangs on the Church's judgment, and that its authority, testimony, and consent are the rule and plumbline by which all Scripture must be tested so we can be sure of it — citing Augustine's famous line, I would not believe the Gospel unless the Catholic Church's authority moved me.

And elsewhere the same holy man: The faithful mind will keep this measure in the Canonical Scriptures — prefer what all Catholic churches receive to what some refuse; and among books not received by all, prefer what more and weightier churches receive to what fewer churches of lesser standing hold.

source_text: XXX. Ut omnibus his satis fiat, ante omnia hic est in memoriam revocandum quid Ecclesiae nomine intelligant adversarii. Id enim apprime necessarium est ad statum quaestionis probe intelligendum, & tollendam hic omnem homonymiam. Igitur sciendum est Ecclesiam hic non sumi collective pro tota multitudine fidelium qui sunt & hactenus fuerunt. Nec enim de istius Ecclesiae authoritate proprie quaestio est. Et quamvis Scripturae sacrae authoritas nequidem ex Ecclesiae sic sumptae authoritate pendeat, certum est tamen ex ejus testimonio & consensu duci posse argumentum pro Scripturae authoritate divinum & infallibile, & quod fidem nostram obliget: quandoquidem in ista Ecclesia comprehenditur Apostolica & primitiva, cujus fuit Scripturae Canonem certa quadam & divina ratione confirmare, & fidelibus tradere, tanquam qui deinceps esset unica fidei regula.
english: To answer all this, first recall what the adversaries mean by "Church." That is essential for the real state of the question and for clearing away the ambiguity of the name.
Church is not here taken collectively for the whole multitude of the faithful who are and ever have been. The debate is not properly about that Church's authority.

Even though sacred Scripture's authority does not depend on the authority of the Church so taken, it is still certain that from that Church's testimony and consent one can draw a divine, infallible argument for Scripture's authority that binds our faith — because that Church includes the Apostolic and primitive Church, whose role it was to confirm Scripture's Canon by a sure divine reason and hand it to the faithful as what would thereafter be faith's unique rule.

source_text: XXXI. Pontificii vero per Ecclesiam praesentem intelligunt uniuscujusque saeculi. Nec adhuc per illam Ecclesiam praesentem communitatem fidelium uno eodemque saeculo viventium intelligunt: sed restringunt Ecclesiae nomen ad praepositos & Pastores Ecclesiae. Itaque, quum pertendunt Scripturae authoritatem ab authoritate Ecclesiae pendere, mens eorum est, fidem illam, qua fidelis populus Scripturae libros amplectitur ut veros & divinos, niti testimonio Pastorum qui tum Ecclesiae praesunt, & testimonio illi acquiescere. Et hoc quia in Pastoribus & praesulibus Ecclesiae perpetuo residet infallibilis & divina quaedam authoritas, ex qua de libri alicujus veritate & divinitate pronunciare possint: ita ut sententia & judicium illorum fidem nostram obliget. Imo illos ea esse praeditos potestate, ut liber, qui hactenus dubiae fuit authoritatis, & de quo in utramque partem opinari licuit, per determinationem illorum fiat authenticus, & eodem postea debeat haberi numero quo libri alii sacri & canonici.
english: But by "present Church" the Pontificians mean the Church of each age.
Even then they do not mean the community of the faithful living in one and the same age. They restrict the name "Church" to the overseers and pastors of the Church.

So when they claim that the authority of Scripture depends on the authority of the Church, they mean that the faith by which the faithful people receive the books of Scripture as true and divine rests on the testimony of the pastors then in office, and settles on that testimony.

Why? Because in the pastors and prelates of the Church there always resides a certain infallible, divine authority by which they can decide the truth and divinity of a book, so that their sentence and judgment bind our faith.

They even hold that those pastors have power to make authentic a book that until then was of doubtful authority, and about which either side might be held, so that after their determination it must be ranked with the other sacred and canonical books.

source_text: XXXII. Fuerunt quidem inter veteres Scholasticos qui authoritatem illam de Scriptura infallibiliter & certo determinandi ad Apostolicam Ecclesiam restrinxerunt, & docuerunt non alio sensu tribuendam esse Ecclesiae praesenti, quam quia cum Apostolica censetur unum corpus. Et senex revera fecit quae fecit quum esset puer, licet jam senex non possit amplius illa facere. Quae fuit sententia Durandi, & Thomae Waldensis, & etiam superiori saeculo Driedonis. At haec sententia hodie communiter erronea censetur. Et hodierni Scholae Pontificiae Doctores in priorem illam sententiam concedunt. Itaque videndum est, an ex usu & praxi Ecclesiae, & illis priscorum Patrum argumentationibus, quae supra adductae sunt, concludi possit Pastorum qui unoquoque saeculo Ecclesiam gubernant, authoritatem tantam esse, ut sit fidei nostrae circa Scripturam regula, Scriptura ipsa quoad nos certior & notior, & qua fides nostra de Scriptura sacra, tanquam praecipuo fundamento nitatur. Illud est quod negamus: neque quicquam ad hoc faciunt probationes illae quae supra allatae sunt.
english: Among the older scholastics some did restrict that power of deciding Scripture infallibly and with certainty to the Apostolic Church. They taught that it belongs to the present Church only insofar as that Church is counted one body with the Apostolic — as an old man truly did what he did as a boy, though as an old man he can no longer do those same acts.

That was the view of Durandus, of Thomas Netter of Walden, and in the previous age of Driedo. Today that view is commonly judged wrong, and the doctors of the present Roman schools yield to the earlier opinion instead.

So the question is whether from the Church's practice, and from the ancient Fathers' arguments recited above, one may conclude that the pastors who govern the Church in each age have authority so great that it is our rule of faith about Scripture — more certain and better known to us than Scripture itself — and the chief foundation of our faith in sacred Scripture.
That is what we deny. The proofs already brought do nothing to establish it.

source_text: XXXIII. Ultro quidem concedimus Doctores Ecclesiae antiquae eo nomine rejecisse libros Apocryphos, quos haeretici confinxerant, & pro divinis obtrudebant, quod libri illi nunquam in Canone Ecclesiae fuerint, neque a Doctoribus Ecclesiae agniti, & pro divinis habiti & citati. Et hanc eorum argumentationem tanquam legitimam probamus, & simili plane modo impugnamos authoritatem librorum illorum quos Ecclesia Romana adjicit ad Vetus Testamentum supra Ecclesiae Judaicae Canonem: nempe, quia hi libri nunquam ab Ecclesia Judaica agniti fuerunt, etiam tum quum vera & sola esset Dei Ecclesia. Imo nec a primitiva Ecclesia Christiana, cujus Doctores communi consensu, paucissimis forte quibusdam exceptis, libros illos e Canone expungunt, licet eorum lectionem in Ecclesiis admittant, tanquam utilem ad plebis aedificationem. Et quamvis libri plerique Apocryphi notas quasdam in se vanitatis habeant, & infirmitatis humanae vestigia, quibus deprehendi possit illos a Deo inspiratos non esse: tamen absolute & in genere loquendo, non putamus ullum esse magis idoneum argumentum, quo librorum Apocryphorum authoritas infringi possit, quam quod nunquam vera Dei Ecclesia eos pro divinis habuerit.
english: We gladly grant that the doctors of the ancient Church rejected the apocryphal books heretics had forged and pushed as divine on this ground: those books were never in the Church's Canon, nor acknowledged, held, and cited as divine by the Church's doctors.

We treat that argument as sound, and we use the same kind of argument against the books Rome adds to the Old Testament beyond the Jewish Canon — because the Jewish Church never acknowledged them, even while it was still God's true and only Church.

Nor did the primitive Christian Church: its doctors, by common consent (a very few perhaps excepted), remove those books from the Canon, though they allow them to be read in churches as useful for the people's edification.

Many apocryphal books do carry marks of vanity and traces of human weakness that show they are not God-inspired. Still, speaking absolutely and in general, we judge no argument more fit to break their authority than this: the true Church of God never held them as divine.

source_text: XXXIV. Sed ut subsistat argumentum istud, & vim suam habeat, non necesse est ut praesentis Ecclesiae Pastores authoritatem habeant divinam & infallibilem, Scriptura ipsa quoad nos notiorem & superiorem. Nec argumentum istud simpliciter nititur eorum authoritate: sed vis argumenti in eo consistit, quod, si libri illi Apocryphi vere divini essent, & a Prophetis & Apostolis eo fine conscripti, ut perpetua essent in Ecclesia fidei regula, proculdubio a Prophetis & Apostolis ipsis pro talibus traditi & commendati fidelibus essent, ut alii libri Canonici, & cum reliquo Scripturae Canone consignati. At si hoc factum esset, Apostolici viri & Ecclesia proxime succedens Apostolis, quae tanta reverentia reliquos eorum libros suscepit, absque omni dubio istos quoque suscepisset, &, si non ab omnibus, saltem a maxima, aut notabili parte fidelium admissi fuissent. Itaque quod eorum ne meminerint quidem prisci Ecclesiae Doctores, signum est manifestum Apostolos, quum Canonem Scripturae consignarunt, ejusmodi libros non admisisse, sed rejecisse & repudiasse. Nec ullo modo verisimile est Deum singulari sua providentia Prophetam aut Apostolum ad scribendum impulisse, eo fine ut liber illius esset fidei regula in Ecclesia Dei, & ad eruditionem & consolationem fidelium inserviret, & tamen passum fuisse ut liber ille ab Ecclesia sua nec reciperetur nec agnosceretur.
english: For that argument to stand, the pastors of the present Church need not have a divine, infallible authority better known to us and superior to Scripture itself.

The argument does not simply rest on their authority. Its force is this: if those apocryphal books were truly divine, and written by the prophets and apostles to be a perpetual rule of faith in the Church, the prophets and apostles themselves would without doubt have handed them down and recommended them as such — like the other canonical books, and sealed with the rest of Scripture's Canon.

Had that happened, the apostolic men and the Church next after the apostles, which received their other books with such reverence, would without doubt have received these too — if not among all the faithful, at least among the greatest or a notable part.
That the ancient Church doctors do not even mention them is a clear sign that the apostles, when they sealed Scripture's Canon, did not admit such books, but rejected and cast them out.

It is in no way likely that God by His singular providence moved a prophet or apostle to write so that his book would be a rule of faith and serve the faithful's instruction and comfort — and yet allowed His Church neither to receive nor to acknowledge that book.

source_text: XXXV. Ad secundam vero illam probationem petitam ex libris de quibus olim dubitatum est, quasi librorum quorundam divinorum fuerit olim dubia authoritas, quoniam Ecclesia super illis sententiam suam nondum pronunciarat: postea vero omnis dubitatio sublata fuerit per Ecclesiae judicium & definitionem: Dico primo librorum qui vere divini & Canonici sunt authoritatem nunquam ita fuisse dubiam, ut de iis aliquando dubitare licuerit, amplius vero non liceat, quod Pontificii volunt. Etenim qui dubitarunt de Epistola ad Hebraeos, & Joannis Apocalypsi, aliisque Novi Testamenti libris, id temere fecerunt, & sine justa ratione. Et sicut hodie culpa non careret qui librorum illorum authoritatem negaret, aut in dubium vocaret, ita quoque fuerunt reprehensione digni, qui libris istis olim authoritatem sustulerunt, aut dubios eos reddere voluerunt. Quod attinet autem caeteros illos libros, quos ad Veteris Testamenti Canonem Pontificii pertinere volunt, & de quibus tamen agnoscunt licuisse olim dubitare, quemadmodum merito de illis dubitatum fuit, ita quoque hodie jure dubitari posse contendimus.
english: Next, their second proof from books once doubted — as if certain divine books were once of doubtful authority because the Church had not yet spoken, and all doubt later fell by the Church's judgment and definition.
I say first: the authority of books that are truly divine and canonical was never so doubtful that it was once lawful to doubt them and later unlawful, which is what the Pontificians claim.

Those who doubted Hebrews, John's Apocalypse, and other New Testament books did so rashly and without just cause. Just as today anyone who denied or questioned those books' authority would not be blameless, so those who once stripped them of authority or tried to make them doubtful deserved blame.

But as for the other books Rome wants in the Old Testament Canon, about which they themselves grant it was once lawful to doubt: as they were rightly doubted then, so we contend they may rightly be doubted still.

source_text: XXXVI. Secundo vero dico, nullorum librorum, qui vere divini sint, authoritatem unquam ita fuisse dubiam, ut omnes & passim de iis dubitarint. Sed dubitatio illa quorundam tantum fuit: apud reliquos vero eorum fuit certa authoritas. Ita verum est quidem Epistolam ad Hebraeos, Epistolam Jacobi, & Joannis Apocalypsin, quibusdam fuisse suspectas, & a quibusdam habitas pro supposititiis: attamen apud plerasque Ecclesias authoritatem suam semper obtinuerunt. Nec ullum tempus assignari potest quo non in magna orbis Christiani parte receptae fuerint, & pro divinis & authenticis habitae. Quod indicant ipsa loca quae referunt adversarii tanquam suae causae faventia. Ita negantibus Arianis authoritatem Epistolae ad Hebraeos respondet Theodoretus, Oportebat eos, si non aliud, certe diuturnitatem temporis revereri, quo hanc Epistolam in Ecclesiis perpetuo legerant veritatis alumni. Et sic Apocalypsin adversus Marcionem tuetur Tertullianus, Habemus & Joannis alumnas Ecclesias, nam etsi Apocalypsin ejus Marcion respuit, ordo tamen Episcoporum ad originem recensitus in Joannem stabit authorem. Quod vero spectat Epistolam Jacobi, idem ille Eusebius qui dicit illam quibusdam videri νόθον, adulterinam esse, testatus eam in quamplurimis Ecclesiis fuisse publice receptam.
english: Second: no truly divine book's authority was ever so doubtful that everyone everywhere doubted it. The doubt belonged only to some; among the rest their authority stayed certain.

Hebrews, James, and John's Apocalypse were indeed suspect to some, and by some treated as spurious — yet among most churches they always kept their authority. No time can be named when they were not received in a large part of the Christian world and held divine and authentic.

The very passages the adversaries quote as favoring them show this. Against Arians who denied Hebrews, Theodoret says they ought at least to reverence the long stretch of time in which the truth's pupils had continually read that epistle in the churches.

So Tertullian defends the Apocalypse against Marcion: we also have John's foster-churches; though Marcion rejects his Apocalypse, the line of bishops traced back to the origin will still stand on John as author.
As for James, the same Eusebius who says some thought it νόθον — spurious — also testifies that it was publicly received in very many churches.

source_text: XXXVII. Dico tertio, eos, qui de libris illis dubitarunt, dubitandi causam non habuisse, quod eos non viderent ab Ecclesiis receptos, & antiquorum Patrum eos ad Apostolos authores referentium traditione commendari: sed quod, re non satis expensa, putarent in his libris quaedam esse quae non redolerent divinum Spiritum; nec satis cohaererent cum fidei doctrina reliquis libris comprehensa. Ita dubitatum est in Ecclesia Latina de Epist. ad Hebraeos, quod capite sexto & decimo videretur favere Novatianis, qui lapsis post baptismum omnem spem veniae tollebant. Apocalypsis etiam suspecta fuit propter Millenarios, qui quibusdam ejus locis abuttebantur, quae ipsis in speciem favent. Judae vero Epistola a quibusdam rejecta fuit, quoniam videtur citare librum quendam Apocryphum, qui sub nomine Enoch Patriarchae olim circumferabatur.
english: Third: those who doubted those books did not doubt because they failed to see them received by the churches and recommended by the ancient Fathers' tradition naming the apostles as authors.

They doubted because, without weighing the matter enough, they thought those books contained things that did not savor of the divine Spirit and did not cohere well enough with the faith taught in the other books.
So the Latin Church doubted Hebrews, because chapters six and ten seemed to favor the Novatians, who cut off all hope of pardon from those who fell after baptism.
The Apocalypse was also suspect because of the Millenarians, who misused certain places that seemed to favor them.
Jude was rejected by some because it seems to cite an apocryphal book that once circulated under the name of Enoch the patriarch.

source_text: XXXVIII. Denique quod isti libri communi postea consensu recepti fuerunt, in causa non fuit novum quoddam Ecclesiae decretum, quo sancita fuerit eorum authoritas; sed quae in istis libris scrupulum quibusdam movebant paulatim lucem accipientibus, & probe intellectis, tandem desierunt esse qui dubitarent, & concesserunt omnes in sententiam priscorum Patrum, qui Apostolis proximi, hos libros tanquam ab iis acceptos posteris commendârunt: & frequenti usu atque lectione comprobarunt. Et certe quod istud non sit tribuendum Synodo Laodicenae, aut tertiae Carthaginiensi, patet, quia Synodi illae provinciales fuerunt, nec poterant, ex ipsa adversariorum sententia, fidem proprie obligare. Et revera de istis libris post Synodum Laodicenam dubitatum adhuc fuit. Nam tempore Hieronymi, qui fuit illa recentior, erant adhuc qui dubitarent. Praesertim vero manifestum est, nec Synodum Carthaginiensem, nec Decreta PP. Gelasii & Innocentii, sustulisse dubitationem circa Veteris Testamenti libros, quos Canonicos illi, nos Apocryphos putamus: quandoquidem usque ad Concilii Tridentini tempora, plurimi fuerunt, in ipsa Ecclesia Romana, qui librorum istorum authoritatem rejecerunt.
english: Finally, those books were later received by common consent — not because some new Church decree sanctioned their authority.

What had raised scruple in them gradually came into the light and was rightly understood; at last the doubters ceased, and all conceded to the ancient Fathers nearest the apostles, who recommended these books to later ages as received from them and confirmed them by frequent use and reading.
This cannot be credited to the Synod of Laodicea or the third council of Carthage: those synods were provincial, and on the adversaries' own view could not properly bind the faith.
In fact doubt about those books remained after Laodicea. In Jerome's day — later than that synod — some still doubted.

Above all, neither Carthage nor the decrees of Popes Gelasius and Innocent removed doubt about the Old Testament books they call canonical and we call apocryphal: right up to Trent, many inside the Roman Church itself rejected those books' authority.

source_text: XXXIX. Ad illam vero argumenti confirmationem, quae inde petita est quod Ecclesiae Doctores, ad confutandos varios haereticos, qui quosdam Scripturae libros repudiabant, perpetuo usi sunt testimonio & consensu Ecclesiae, quo librorum istorum authoritatem comprobarunt: Respondeo, inde minime concludi posse quod Pontificii volunt, & quod in quaestione est, nempe authoritatem Pastorum, qui unoquoque saeculo Ecclesiam gubernant, majorem quoad nos & notiorem esse Scripturae authoritate, fidemque nostram de Scriptura niti testimonio & judicio Pastorum qui jam Ecclesiae praesunt tanquam divino & infallibili, & tanquam praecipuo & proprio suo fundamento. Neque Doctores isti simpliciter argumentantur ex Episcoporum sui temporis authoritate, quasi regula fidei fuisset, & ea singulorum Ecclesiae membrorum fides obstringeretur: sed, quum haeretici illi, quos impugnabant, librorum quorundam sacrorum authoritatem rejicerent, quasi Apostolis aut viris Apostolicis falso tribuerentur, & a Catholicis Doctoribus conficti essent, Patres illis opposuerunt perpetuum Episcoporum atque fidelium consensum, qui jam inde ab Apostolorum temporibus, libros illos venerati sunt tanquam ab Apostolis traditos & commendatos pro veris & divinis: cui consensui fidem derogare non potest, nisi homo protervus & pervicax. Etenim, si ille qui hodie negaret libros Aristotelis, Demosthenis & Ciceronis, eorum esse quibus tribuuntur, convinci posset ex consensu Doctorum, qui omnibus saeculis libros illos tribuerunt magnis illis & praestantibus viris, & insanus haberetur qui famae tam constanti & celebri fidem denegaret: Annon pari, imo longe majori jure insanus habeatur, qui se audet opponere traditioni, & famae constantiori & celebriori, & magis adhuc continuae, quae libros illos, quos pro sacris habemus, ad Apostolos refert tanquam authores & approbatores?
english: As for that supporting point — that the Church's doctors, when they answered heretics who rejected certain books of Scripture, kept using the Church's testimony and consensus to prove those books' authority — I answer that this does not yield what the Pontificians want, or what is actually in dispute.

It does not show that the pastors who govern the Church in each age have, for us, an authority greater and better known than Scripture's, or that our faith about Scripture rests on the testimony and judgment of the pastors now in office as on a divine, infallible, chief, and proper foundation.
Those fathers were not simply arguing from the authority of the bishops of their own day as if that were a rule of faith binding every church member.

The heretics they opposed rejected certain sacred books as falsely ascribed to the apostles or apostolic men and as inventions of Catholic teachers. Against that charge the Fathers set the perpetual consensus of bishops and of the faithful who, from the apostles' time on, have received those books as handed down and recommended by the apostles as true and divine.

Only a shameless, stubborn person can refuse that consensus. Anyone today who denied that the books of Aristotle, Demosthenes, and Cicero belong to the men named on them could be answered from the continuous judgment of the learned who have always ascribed them so — and would be thought mad for refusing so constant a fame.

By equal — indeed by far greater — right, then, is the person mad who dares to oppose a tradition and fame still more constant, celebrated, and continuous, which refers the books we hold sacred to the apostles as their authors and approvers?

source_text: XL. Et certe in eo vim praecipue fecisse priscos Ecclesiae Doctores, quum ex authoritate Ecclesiae librorum Canonicorum authoritatem tutati sunt, patet ex Augustino, qui libr. 32. & 33. adversus Faustum Manichaeum, Quaerenti Fausto unde sciret Apostolorum esse istas literas, respondet inde se scire, unde sciebat Faustus literas illas alias esse Manichaei, & unde sciebant omnes libros quosdam esse Varronis, Platonis & Aristotelis, & unde scitura erat posteritas libros quos tunc scribebat Augustinus, esse Augustini. Et postquam plura ejusmodi exempla explicuit & accumulavit, tandem concludit in haec verba, Quae cum ita sint, quis tandem tanto furore caecatur, nisi daemoniorum mendaciloquorum malitia atque fallacia consentiendo subversus sit, qui dicat hoc mereri non potuisse Apostolorum Ecclesiam, tam fidam, tam numerosam fratrum concordiam, ut eorum scripta fideliter ad posteros trajicerent, cum eorum cathedras usque ad praesentes Episcopos certissima successione servaverint, cum hoc qualiumcunque hominum scriptis, sive extra Ecclesiam, sive in ipsa Ecclesia, tam feliciter proveniat.
english: That the early Church doctors put their chief force here when they defended the authority of the canonical books from the Church's authority is plain from Augustine.

In books 32 and 33 against Faustus the Manichee, when Faustus asks how Augustine knows those letters are the apostles', Augustine answers: from the same kind of public knowledge by which Faustus knows other letters are Mani's, by which everyone knows certain books are Varro's, Plato's, or Aristotle's, and by which later ages would know the books Augustine was then writing were his.

After heaping up more such examples he concludes: That being so, who is blinded by such madness — unless overturned by consenting to the malice and deceit of lying demons — who would say the apostles' Church, so faithful and so numerous in brotherly concord, could not have deserved to hand their writings faithfully to later ages, when they have kept their chairs by most certain succession down to the bishops now sitting, and when even ordinary men's writings, inside or outside the Church, fare so well?

source_text: XLI. Itaque quum liber aliquis Scripturae in controversiam vocatur, & dubitatur an vere sit Propheticus & Apostolicus, & cum caetero Canone consignatus ab Apostolis aut viris Apostolicis, agnoscimus optimum hujus rei argumentum duci posse ab Ecclesiae perpetuo & constanti consensu & testimonio, quo liber ille semper relatus est ad Apostolos ut authores sive approbatores, cui testimonio fides derogari non potest, absque magna impudentia atque pervicacia. Nec ullum putamus esse argumentum magis idoneum quo revinci possit homo sectarius, sive haereticus. Nec tamen argumentum istud est divinum, sed humanum, neque vis ejus in eo consistit, quod in Ecclesiae praepositis resideat infallibilis & divina quaedam authoritas. Id enim necesse non est ut argumentum subsistat, & vim suam habeat. Nam in iis qui rem literariam tractant nulla fingi potest talis judicandi infallibilis authoritas. Et tamen perpetuus literatorum consensus qui libros quosdam ascribit Aristoteli, Platoni, & Galeno, sufficit ad plenam fidem faciendam; & si quis contra niti vellet, jure merito protervus & insanus haberetur. Quanto magis ergo consensus Ecclesiae, quam non est dubium peculiari Dei providentia, & Spiritus sancti assistentia regi, fidem faciet librum hunc vel illum ab Apostolo vel Propheta conscriptum, & pro divino commendatum esse.
english: So when a book of Scripture is disputed — whether it is truly prophetic and apostolic, and was sealed with the rest of the canon by the apostles or apostolic men — we grant that the best argument is the Church's perpetual, constant consensus and testimony, which has always referred that book to the apostles as authors or approvers.
Faith cannot be withdrawn from that witness without great shamelessness and stubbornness. We know no fitter argument for answering a sectarian or a heretic.
Yet the argument is human, not divine. Its force does not lie in some infallible, divine authority residing in the Church's overseers. That is not required for the argument to stand.

In literary questions no such infallible judging-authority can even be invented; yet the continuous consensus of the learned that ascribes certain books to Aristotle, Plato, or Galen is enough for full confidence, and anyone who fought it would rightly be thought shameless and mad.

How much more, then, does the Church's consensus — which no one doubts is ruled by God's special providence and the Spirit's help — give us confidence that this or that book was written by an apostle or prophet and recommended as divine.

source_text: XLII. Sed quantumvis bonum & validum argumentum sumi possit ex Ecclesiae consensu & testimonio pro libri alicujus sacri divinitate comprobanda, negamus inde sequi authoritatem Scripturae ab authoritate Ecclesiae pendere tanquam notiori & superiori. Quod ab ipsis adversariis vel maxime invitis extorquere possumus. Nam quemadmodum Patres refellerunt haereticos qui Scripturam negabant ex authoritate & testimonio Ecclesiae; ita quoque Schismaticos veram Ecclesiam Christi non agnoscentes ad Scripturas revocarunt, & ex iis veram Ecclesiam demonstrandam esse contenderunt. Sic enim Augustinus cum Donatistis agit, utrum ipsi Ecclesiam teneant nonnisi divinarum Scripturarum Canonicis libris ostendant. Et hodie Pontificii Ecclesiam suam, & ejus authoritatem ex Scripturis probare conantur: Et eo se officio egregie defungi putant. Et tamen minime volunt Ecclesiae authoritatem quoad nos minus notam & certam esse Scripturae authoritate: quod est ipsum de quo hic quaeritur, & quod affirmamus, illi vero negant. Igitur ex eo quod Scripturae liber aliquis in dubium vocatus, non potest aptiori & certiori argumento contra haereticos defendi, quam ex Ecclesiae consensu & testimonio, Pontificii concludere non possunt authoritatem Ecclesiae certiorem quoad nos & notiorem esse Scripturae authoritate: quandoquidem fateri coguntur haereticum, qui veram Ecclesiam non agnoscit, non posse certiori & firmiori argumento revinci quam Scripturae authoritate. Et tamen ab eo maxime abhorrent ut dicant Scripturae sacrae authoritatem quoad nos authoritate Ecclesiae priorem & notiorem esse.
english: However good and valid an argument may be drawn from the Church's consensus and testimony to prove a sacred book's divinity, we deny that Scripture's authority therefore depends on the Church's as on something better known and superior.

We can force this even from unwilling adversaries. Just as the Fathers answered heretics who denied Scripture from the Church's authority and testimony, they also sent schismatics who would not own Christ's true Church back to the Scriptures, and held that the true Church must be shown from them.

So Augustine with the Donatists: whether they hold the Church, let them show it only by the canonical books of the divine Scriptures. Today the Pontificians try to prove their Church and its authority from Scripture, and think they do that office well.
Yet they refuse to allow that, for us, the Church's authority is less known and certain than Scripture's — which is exactly the point under inquiry: we affirm it; they deny it.

So from the fact that a disputed book of Scripture has no fitter or surer defense against heretics than the Church's consensus and testimony, they cannot conclude that the Church's authority is for us more certain and better known than Scripture's.

They themselves must admit that a heretic who does not acknowledge the true Church cannot be answered by any firmer argument than Scripture's authority — and yet they most of all shrink from saying that sacred Scripture's authority is for us prior to and better known than the Church's.

source_text: XLIII. Itaque dicendum est non omnes probationes ab eo sumi quod est simpliciter notius & certius. Etenim inter disputandum cogimur nos attemperare illis, quibuscum nobis res est: Et contra eos qui principia negant, & ea quae sunt in se certissima, uti minus certis probationibus, & argumentis illis quae vocantur a posteriori, hoc est, quibus quod est cognitione prius, simpliciter loquendo, probatur per illud quod est cognitione posterius. Sic contra Ethnicos qui negant religionem Christianam, argumentamur saepe ex placitis sapientum, philosophicis axiomatibus, & consensu gentium. Et tamen omnia ista tantam respectu nostri certitudinem non habent, quam religio Christiana. Et ipsa prima principia, quibus absolute nihil est notius & certius, probamus exemplis & inductionibus, unde tamen non pendet principiorum illorum certitudo & authoritas.
english: So not every proof is taken from what is simply better known and more certain.

In dispute we must adapt to those we are dealing with. Against people who deny principles — even things most certain in themselves — we use weaker proofs and arguments called a posteriori: proving what is prior in knowledge, simply speaking, through what is posterior in knowledge.

Against Gentiles who deny the Christian religion we often argue from the opinions of the wise, from philosophical axioms, and from the nations' consensus — yet none of that has, for us, as much certainty as the Christian religion itself.
Even first principles, than which nothing is absolutely better known or more certain, we illustrate by examples and inductions; but their certainty and authority do not depend on those illustrations.

source_text: XLIV. In summa ergo fatemur authoritatem librorum sacrorum per Ecclesiae consensum & testimonium recte & valide probari. Sed negamus tamen inde sequi quod adversarii volunt, nempe Ecclesiae testimonium esse regulam fidei Scriptura ipsa notiorem quoad nos. Non enim omnis bona probatio ex aliqua fidei regula & principio sumitur, nec etiam ex eo quod est simpliciter notius & certius: sed saepe res probare cogimur ad hominem, & a posteriori.
english: In short, then: we grant that the sacred books' authority is rightly and validly proved by the Church's consensus and testimony.
We deny what the adversaries infer — that the Church's testimony is a rule of faith better known to us than Scripture itself.
Not every sound proof is taken from a rule and principle of faith, or even from what is simply better known and more certain. Often we must prove the point to the person before us, and a posteriori.

source_text: I. Ecclesiarum, quae secessionem ab Ecclesia Romana fecerunt superiori saeculo, constans sententia est, Scripturam sacram, omnia quae ad fidem & salutem pertinent, sufficienter continere: ita ut opus non sit alio Dei verbo, unde ea, quae desunt Scripturae, suppleantur. Ecclesiae vero Romanae Doctores & propugnatores sententiam illam acerrime impugnant, estque ea de re gravis controversia, quam hisce thesibus & sequentibus aliquot tractare aggredimur. Ut autem distinctius & clarius id fiat, Ecclesiarum nostrarum sententiam quam dilucide & distincte a nobis fieri poterit exponemus. Deinde inquiremus in sententiam adversariorum, illamque cum nostra conferentes, manifestum reddemus quid proprie sit illud quod in quaestione est. Ac denique veritatem paucis confirmabimus, & adversae sententiae fundamenta subruemus.
english: The Churches that left Rome in the last century hold this steadily: sacred Scripture sufficiently contains everything that belongs to faith and salvation — so that we do not need another word of God to fill what Scripture supposedly lacks.
Rome’s doctors and champions attack that claim fiercely. The dispute is serious; we take it up in these theses and a few that follow.

For clarity we will first state our Churches’ view as plainly as we can, then compare the adversaries’ view with ours so the real question stands out, and finally confirm the truth briefly and undercut the opposite case.

source_text: II. Quod ad primum attinet, ante omnia nostri Theologi distinguunt inter ea quae sunt ad salutem necessaria, & ea quae ad salutem necessaria non sunt. Et quidem ea quae sunt ad salutem necessaria Scriptura sacra contineri asserunt. Ea vero quae non sunt ad salutem necessaria, ex eorum mente Scriptura contineri nihil necesse est.
english: First our theologians distinguish what is necessary to salvation from what is not.
They hold that Scripture contains what is necessary to salvation. What is not necessary need not, on their view, be in Scripture at all.

source_text: III. Sed hic observandum est aliquid ad salutem necessarium dici posse duobus modis. Et primo quidem quoniam tale est, ut nemo illud ignorare queat citra salutis dispendium, neque possit ullus servari sine expressa ejus cognitione. Deinde etiam quia nullus illud rejicere potest, & contrarium ejus Ecclesia docere, quin peccet in propriam salutem.
english: ‘Necessary to salvation’ is said in two ways.
First: no one may be ignorant of it without losing salvation, and no one is saved without express knowledge of it.
Second: no one may reject it, or have the Church teach its contrary, without sinning against his own salvation.

source_text: IV. Et similiter aliquid ad fidem necessarium dicitur, vel quia necessarium est ad singulorum fidem, nec quisquam sine fide illius explicita fidelis censeri debet: vel in genere ad objectum fidei pertinet, & publicam fidem Ecclesiae obligat.
english: So also ‘necessary to faith’ has two senses.
Either it is required for each person’s faith — no one without explicit faith in it should be counted a believer — or it belongs in general to faith’s object and binds the Church’s public faith.

source_text: V. Quum autem statuunt Ecclesiae nostrae ea, quae sunt ad fidem & salutem necessaria, in Scripturis omnia haberi, intelligunt necessaria non tantum primo modo, sed etiam secundo modo. Nec enim id solum volumus, extra Scripturam nihil esse sine cujus explicita fide & notitia ad salutem nemo pervenire possit: sed hoc quoque, neminem existimari debere in fidem Christianam, & salutem propriam peccare, eo quod rejiciat & impugnet aliquid quod Scriptura sacra non docet. Unde sequitur nostram sententiam non satis probari, inductione facta eorum quorum fides & cognitio explicita possit alicui ad salutem sufficere. Nam fides in genere ambitu suo plura comprehendit, quam ea quorum cognitio ad salutem necessaria sit. Ad fidem autem nihil pertinere censemus quod in Scriptura non reperiatur.
english: When our Churches say Scripture has everything necessary to faith and salvation, they mean necessary in both senses — not the first alone.

We do not only claim that nothing outside Scripture is such that without explicit faith and knowledge of it no one can be saved. We also claim that no one should be judged to sin against Christian faith and his own salvation merely for rejecting and attacking what sacred Scripture does not teach.

So our case is not proved by listing only what explicit faith for salvation needs. Faith’s scope is wider than that minimum — yet we still hold that nothing belongs to faith that Scripture does not contain.

source_text: VI. Ideoque ut vitetur omnis ambiguitas, nonnulli ex nostris Theologis utuntur hac distinctione clariori & commodiori. Observant enim distinguendum esse inter ea in quibus substantia est, & quasi corpus religionis Christianae, & quae ex vi divinae institutionis necessaria sunt non tantum ad fidem, sed etiam ad mores formandos, politiamque Ecclesiae continendam: & alia quae sunt tantum hujus substantiae veluti appendices, & corporis hujus ornamenta, quaeque nec ex natura sua, nec ex divina institutione, necessaria sunt, sed indifferentia, ordinisque tantum & decoris gratia in usum recepta: ut sunt multae disciplinae partes variis Canonibus sancitae, ritus etiam & caeremoniae variae, tum universales, tum particulares, observationis liberae quidem, sed hactenus ut nemo sua privata authoritate illa possit aut debeat contemnere rejicereve.
english: To cut ambiguity, some of our theologians prefer a clearer distinction.

They separate what is the substance — the body of Christian religion — necessary by divine institution not only for faith but for morals and church order, from mere appendages and ornaments of that body.

Those ornaments are not necessary by nature or divine institution; they are indifferent, kept for order and decency: many disciplinary canons, and rites and ceremonies universal or particular — freely observed, yet not to be despised or dropped by private authority alone.

source_text: VII. Res prioris generis asserimus sacra Scriptura contineri, non item alias istas, quae sunt ad Ecclesiae fidem, mores & disciplinam veluti accidentariae. Multa enim quae pertinent ad varias divini cultus & Ecclesiasticae politiae circumstantias, fatemur non esse sigillatim in Scriptura tradita, sed relicta prudentiae praepositorum Ecclesiae, sub hoc generali praecepto, ut omnia fiant ordine & decenter in Ecclesia Dei. Unde patet ab Ecclesiae Romanae Doctoribus frustra contra nos in hac controversia, varias instantias peti a ritibus, statutis & caeremoniis quibusdam, quae in Ecclesia antiqua, sive judaica sive Christiana, olim observata sunt, & etiamnum apud nos servantur tam in divino cultu, quam in politia Ecclesiastica, etiamsi nihil de iis in Scriptura constitutum sit.
english: We say Scripture contains the former kind — the substance — not those accidental appendages of church faith, morals, and discipline.

Many circumstances of worship and church polity are not set out item by item in Scripture; they are left to the prudence of church overseers under the general rule that all things be done decently and in order in God’s Church.

So Rome’s doctors waste their shot when they press old Jewish or Christian rites, statutes, and ceremonies — still kept among us in worship and polity — as if their absence from a Scripture catalogue refuted us.

source_text: VIII. Igitur quae sint illa, quae Scriptura sacra contineri dicimus, ex dictis manifestum est. Deinceps videndum est, qua ratione & modo ex sententia nostra in Scriptura contineantur. Porro dogmata & praecepta quaedam in aliquo libro possunt contineri duobus modis. Primo quidem κατὰ λέξιν, & iisdem verbis. Secundo in substantia, & verbis aequipollentibus. Nostra autem sententia non est omnia fidei dogmata, atque vitae praecepta quae traduntur ab orthodoxis, totidem verbis in sacra Scriptura reperiri. Istud quidem nobis imputant hodierni quidam vitilitigatores, qui ex eo quod profitemur nihil nos extra Scripturam in religionis negotio suscipere, exigunt ut quaecunque scribimus & docemus, totidem verbis & syllabis in Scriptura sacra ostendamus. Verum nobis sufficit ad credendum aliquod dogma, ut Scriptura sacra illud in substantia contineat. Ita Scriptura Sacra nullibi habet haec verba, Deus est unus & trinus. Et tamen illud certa fide credimus, quin quod eodem recidit Scriptura dicit tres esse in caelo, Patrem, Verbum, & Spiritum, & hos tres unum esse. Et pluribus in locis testatur Deum esse unum, & tamen Patrem esse Deum, Filium esse Deum, & Spiritum sanctum esse Deum.
english: From the above it is clear what we say Scripture contains. Next: how it contains them.
Dogmas and precepts may stand in a book in two ways — first κατὰ λέξιν, in the same words; second in substance, in equivalent words.

We do not claim every orthodox dogma and life-precept appears in Scripture in so many words. Some modern wranglers pin that on us: because we take up nothing outside Scripture in religion, they demand every sentence we teach be shown syllable by syllable in the text.

For us it is enough that Scripture contain the dogma in substance. Scripture nowhere says the bare words ‘God is one and three’; yet we believe it firmly, because Scripture says what comes to the same — three in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Spirit, and these three are one — and in many places that God is one, while the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each God.

source_text: IX. Priori autem isti distinctioni affinis est altera. Nam aliud est continere expresse & immediate, aliud mediate & per consequentiam. Et Scriptura quidem, ex nostrorum mente, omnia fidei dogmata non continet immediate & expresse. Sed nihil est ad fidem & religionem necessario pertinens, quod ex Scriptura deduci non possit per bonam & apertam consequentiam. Sic non dicit expresse Scriptura, Christum duas naturas habere, & in eo duas esse voluntates. Attamen ad fidei veritatem utrumque pertinet: quoniam aperte ex eo consequitur, quod Scriptura docet pluribus in locis, nempe, Christum verum Deum, & verum hominem esse.
english: Beside the last distinction stands another close to it. One thing is to contain a teaching expressly and immediately; another is to contain it mediately, by consequence.

On our view Scripture does not hold every dogma of faith in that immediate, express form. Still nothing that necessarily belongs to faith and religion fails to follow from Scripture by a good, open consequence.

Scripture never says in so many words that Christ has two natures, or two wills in him. Both still belong to the truth of faith, because they follow openly from what Scripture teaches in many places — that Christ is true God and true man.

source_text: X. Unde patet rursus hodiernos Sophistas injuste nos vexare, quum aliquod dogma nostrum per bonam consequentiam ex Scriptura eruimus. Quasi in eo retigeremus legem a nobis positam, qua statuimus Scripturam unicam esse fidei & religionis regulam, cui nihil addendum, nihil detrahendum sit. Nam ex Scriptura aliquid deducere non est ei aliquid addere, aut aliam fidei regulam substituere: sed illa ipsa quae continet evolvere, & reconditos ejus thesauros explicare. Ita dicuntur in Actis Prophetae Christo attestari, fore ut qui credit in eum remissionem peccatorum per nomen ejus accipiat. Neque tamen istud ullibi expresse positum, reperitur apud Prophetas; Sed dicuntur Prophetae testari quod ex testimoniis eorum deducitur.
english: So today's Sophists wrong us when they chide us for drawing a dogma from Scripture by good consequence — as if we broke our own law that Scripture alone is the rule of faith and religion, with nothing added or taken away.
To deduce from Scripture is not to add to it, nor to put another rule in its place. It is to unroll what Scripture already holds and to open its hidden stores.

In Acts the Prophets are said to testify of Christ that whoever believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name. Those bare words are not set down expressly in the Prophets; the Prophets are said to testify what follows from their witness.

source_text: XI. Praeterea dogmata quaedam ex aliquo principio deduci possunt duobus modis. Primo sigillatim, distincte & per se. Deinde generatim confuse, & per aliud. Sic omnia religionis Christianae dogmata & instituta ex Scriptura veteris Testamenti probari non possunt per se & sigillatim. Ut, exempli gratia, fideles esse baptizandos in Nomine Patris, Filii, & Spiritus sancti ex veteri Testamento satis probari non posset, si nullum aliud fidei principium suppeteret praeter illam veterem Scripturam. Et tamen omnia quae ad Evangelicam doctrinam pertinent ex veteri Testamento in genere probari possunt, quatenus inde potest efficaciter demonstrari Jesum Nazarenum esse Messiam, & Dei Filium a Prophetis promissum: adeoque doctrinam illius veram & divinam esse, & ejus instituta tanquam divina a nobis amplectenda. Quae generatim & confuse tantum ex aliquo principio colligi, & deduci possunt, in eo continentur virtute atque in semine. Quae vero ex eo probantur distincte & sigillatim expresse dici possunt aliquo modo in eo contineri: licet strictiori sensu expresse idem significet ac diserte & immediate.
english: Dogmas may also be drawn from a principle in two ways: item by item, distinctly and of themselves; or only in a general, mixed way, through something else.

Not every Christian dogma and ordinance can be proved from the Old Testament by itself, one by one. Baptism in the Name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit could not be shown from the Old Testament alone if that were our only principle of faith.

Yet everything that belongs to Gospel teaching can be proved from the Old Testament in general, because from it one can show effectively that Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah and the Son of God promised by the Prophets — and therefore that his teaching is true and divine, and his ordinances to be received as divine.

What follows from a principle only in that general, mixed way is in it by force and in seed. What is proved from it distinctly, item by item, may be said to be in it expressly in a looser sense — though strictly 'expressly' means the same as clearly and immediately.

source_text: XII. In hac autem disputatione sententia nostra non est omnia religionis Christianae instituta, & fidei dogmata confuse solum atque generatim ex Scriptura probari posse sed distincte & sigillatim, adeoque, hoc quidem sensu, dici posse in Scriptura expresse contineri non virtute tantum, atque in semine.
english: In this dispute we do not say Christian ordinances and dogmas of faith can be proved from Scripture only in a general, mixed way.
We say they can be proved distinctly, item by item — and in that sense can be said to stand expressly in Scripture, not merely by force and in seed.

source_text: XIII. Quandoquidem autem omnia quae ad fidem pertinent Scriptura sacra continentur, quomodo jam expositum est, inde colligitur Scripturam esse fidei regulam perfectam & sufficientem. Quae tamen sufficientia non excludit necessitatem ministerii Ecclesiastici, quo, juxta ordinem a Deo constitutum, doctrina caelestis ex Scriptura hauritur, & fideli populo per suos pastores & doctores traditur: tum quoque interni Spiritus magisterii, quo fideles ducuntur in notitiam doctrinae ex Scriptura haustae atque propositae, & sine quo illam discernere, & salutariter amplecti non possunt. Sed ista Scripturae sacrae perfectio & sufficientia, excludit solummodo necessitatem alterius regulae, quam Scripturae sacrae adjungi necesse sit, ut integram fidei doctrinam habeamus. Unde patet nihil agere Ecclesiae Romanae Doctores, qui nobis ad salutem Scripturam non sufficere inde probare conantur, quod alioqui frustra foret ministerium Ecclesiasticum, cujus tamen necessitas in ipsa sacra Scriptura commendatur.
english: Since everything that belongs to faith is in sacred Scripture in the way already shown, Scripture is a perfect and sufficient rule of faith.

That sufficiency does not cancel the Church's ministry. By God's order, heavenly teaching is drawn from Scripture and given to the faithful through their pastors and teachers. It also does not cancel the Spirit's inward teaching, by which believers come to know the doctrine drawn from Scripture and set before them — without which they cannot discern it or embrace it for salvation.
Scripture's perfection and sufficiency shut out only one thing: the need of another rule that must be joined to Scripture before we have the whole doctrine of faith.
So Rome's doctors gain nothing when they argue that Scripture is not enough for salvation because otherwise the Church's ministry would be useless. Scripture itself urges that ministry.

source_text: XIV. Verum ad pleniorem quaestionis hujus intelligentiam, hic quoque est animadvertendum, ea quae in scholis nostris tractari solent, & in publicis nostrorum confessionibus proponi, & exponi, vel consistere in admissione verorum principiorum fidei & religionis, & rejectione eorum quae pro talibus principiis immerito & falso obtruduntur: vel esse doctrinam ipsam ex veris principiis haustam atque deductam. Et fidei quidem principia Scriptura sacra contineri dicimus, quoniam sunt ipsa Scriptura. Nec enim Ecclesiae nostrae ulla fidei principia admittunt, praeter libros divinitus inspiratos quibus constat Scripturae corpus.
english: For a fuller grasp of the question, note what our schools treat and our public confessions set out. Some of it is admitting the true principles of faith and religion, and rejecting what is falsely pushed forward as such. The rest is the doctrine drawn from those true principles.

We say Scripture contains the principles of faith because those principles are Scripture itself. Our Churches admit no principles of faith beyond the inspired books that make up the body of Scripture.

source_text: XV. Sed plenitudo & sufficientia quam Scripturae sacrae tribuimus, nullo modo requirit, ut ex ea fidei principia probari & demonstrari possint, verbi gratia, hunc, aut illum librum divinum esse atque Canonicum. Etenim cujusvis regulae perfectio in eo consistit, ut sit reliquorum omnium quae sunt ejusdem generis mensura, minime vero ut sit regula sui ipsius. Neque in ulla disciplina requiritur in principiis, ut seipsa probent & demonstrent, quod absurdum est & impossibile, sed in suo genere sat perfecta habentur, si ex iis omnia quae ad talem scientiam, & disciplinam pertinent, probari & demonstrari possint.
english: The fullness and sufficiency we give sacred Scripture do not require that Scripture prove its own principles — for example, that this or that book is divine and canonical.
Any rule is perfect when it measures everything else of its kind. It need not be the rule of itself.
No science asks its first principles to prove themselves; that is absurd and impossible. Principles are perfect enough in their kind if from them everything belonging to that science can be proved.

source_text: XVI. Quemadmodum igitur in disciplinis omnibus humanis sunt principia quaedam, unicuique arti & scientiae propria, ex quibus deducuntur & probantur conclusiones & propositiones omnes, quae pertinent ad artem & scientiam cujus sunt principia, ipsa vero in eo genere per se certa sunt nec demonstrari queunt: adeoque dici possunt esse veluti regula unde pendent, & per quam probantur omnia, quae ad talem artem aut scientiam spectant, licet ipsa sese probare nec possint, nec debeant: sic quoque res se habet in divina & caelesti doctrina. Nam quum Theoremata, & propositiones ejus ad examen revocantur, & quaeritur quod sit eorum fundamentum, necessario deveniendum est ad principia quaedam, ultra quae in eo saltem genere, procedi non possit: Ac per consequens, quae non possint per alia fidei principia probari, & a quibus quoque exigi non debet, ut seipsa probent, quandoquidem seipsum nihil probare potest: Et quae tamen haberi debeant pro sufficiente & perfecta fidei regula, quoniam caetera omnia, quae ad fidem pertinent, per ipsa probantur atque demonstrantur.
english: In every human art and science there are first principles proper to that field. From them every conclusion belonging to the art is drawn and proved. The principles themselves are certain in that kind and cannot be demonstrated. They are, as it were, the rule on which the rest hangs — though they neither can nor should prove themselves.
Divine teaching is the same. When its theorems are examined and we ask for their foundation, we must come to principles beyond which, in that kind at least, we cannot go.

Those principles cannot be proved by other principles of faith, and no one should demand that they prove themselves — nothing proves itself. Yet they must be held as a sufficient and perfect rule of faith, because everything else that belongs to faith is proved by them.

source_text: XVII. Ex communi quidem Theologorum sensu, in eo discrimen est inter principia fidei, & principia scientiarum, quod principia scientiarum per se nota sunt, & evidentia, & sua luce assensum extorquent a naturali rationis lumine: principia vero fidei non habent parem evidentiam; ideoque, sicuti par est, credi & suscipi non possunt, nisi per illuminationem internam Spiritus sancti. Attamen in hoc conveniunt, quod sicuti principiis naturalibus assentimur immediate per naturale lumen intellectus, non vero per alia notiora quaedam principia, per quae demonstrata fuerint; ita quoque fidei principiis credimus immediate, per Spiritus sancti illuminationem, non vero interventu probationis alicujus, quae ducta sit ex aliis notioribus in hoc genere principiis.
english: Theologians commonly mark this difference between the principles of faith and the principles of the sciences. Science axioms are known in themselves, evident, and by their own light compel assent from natural reason. Faith principles do not have that same evidence. So, as is right, they cannot be believed and received except through the Holy Spirit's inward illumination.

Yet they agree in this: we assent to natural principles at once by the mind's natural light, not through other better-known principles that prove them. In the same way we believe faith's principles immediately through the Spirit's illumination — not by some intervening proof drawn from other principles more known in that order.

source_text: XVIII. Habere quidem debent prima fidei principia divinitatis & veritatis suae notas & characteres, & argumenta quibus probentur & suadeantur: sed directe & proprie seipsa probare non possunt: nec etiam ab aliis pendent fidei principiis, unde authoritatem & fidem mutuentur. Jam vero prima illa religionis regula, & Christianae fidei principia nobis sunt Scripturae divinae constantes certo numero librorum θεοπνεύστων.
