Ac proinde sacrae Scripturae authoritas, juxta sententiam nostram, ex ipsa Scriptura probari non debet, sed ab omnibus Christianis immediate & propter se suscipi.
english: Faith's first principles must bear marks and characters of their divinity and truth, and arguments that recommend them. But they cannot, directly and properly, prove themselves. Nor do they lean on other faith principles from which they would borrow authority.
That first rule of religion — the principles of Christian faith — is for us the divine Scriptures, a fixed set of God-breathed books (θεοπνεύστων).
So on our view Scripture's authority should not be proved from Scripture itself. All Christians receive it immediately, and for its own sake.

source_text: XIX. Sed quemadmodum, si prima cujusdam scientiae principia negentur ab homine contentioso, non probantur illa ex seipsis, sed illius scientiae fines transire necesse est, & aliunde eorum probationes quaerere: aut etiam recurrere ad quaedam minus nota quibus probentur a posteriori, & ad hominem illum; neque hoc quicquam derogat principiorum illorum perfectioni & sufficientiae: Ita si Scripturarum sacrarum divinitas in dubium vocetur, ut fit ab Ethnicis & profanis hominibus, probanda quidem erit, non tamen ex proprio earum testimonio, aut ex alio quopiam fidei principio, neque amplius suppetunt probationes quas vocant de fide, hoc est, quae petitae sint ex proprie dictis fidei principiis: sed aliae probationes adhibendae erunt, quae petentur ex variis notis, tum intus, tum externis, quibus Scripturae Sacrae divinitas innotescere, & confirmari potest. Neque hoc obstat quominus, fidelium respectu, plenissima sit & perfectissima religionis & fidei regula.
english: If a contentious man denies a science's first principles, you do not prove them from themselves. You must leave that science's bounds and seek proofs elsewhere — or even use weaker, a posteriori arguments aimed at that man. That does not lessen the principles' perfection or sufficiency.

So if Gentiles and profane men call Scripture's divinity into doubt, it must be proved — yet not from Scripture's own testimony, nor from any other faith principle. The proofs called de fide (drawn from faith principles properly so named) no longer apply.

Other proofs must be used: various marks, inward and outward, by which Scripture's divinity can be known and confirmed. That still leaves Scripture, for believers, the fullest and most perfect rule of religion and faith.

source_text: XX. Atque hinc patet quomodo occurrendum sit argumento, quo se plurimum jactant Pontificii, dum, scilicet, se demonstrare putant Scripturam non esse plenam & sufficientem fidei regulam, quoniam ipsa Scriptura per Scripturam probari non potest. Nec enim, ut patet ex dictis, ad perfectionem & sufficientiam regulae requiritur, ut possit seipsam probare. Sed satis est ut per eam examinari & probari possint omnia praeter ipsam quae sunt ejusdem generis. Ac praeterea in fidei analysi, nisi quis velit admittere circulum, aut progressum in infinitum, quorum utrunque absurdum est, necesse est devenire ad principium quoddam in quo sistendum sit, & quod probari non possit per aliud in eo genere notius, nec etiam seipsum probare, quandoquidem, ut dictum est, nihil probat seipsum.
english: Here is how to meet the argument Rome loves: that Scripture is not a full and sufficient rule of faith because Scripture cannot be proved by Scripture.
A rule need not prove itself to be perfect and sufficient. It is enough that by it everything else of the same kind can be examined and proved.

In analyzing faith, unless you allow a circle or an infinite regress — both absurd — you must stop at some principle that cannot be proved by another better known in that order, and that cannot prove itself. Nothing proves itself.

source_text: XXI. Sicut autem ad perfectionem, quam Scripturae sacrae tribuimus, non requiritur, ut seipsam probet, ita quoque nihil necesse est, ut, quae falso obtenduntur fidei principia, per Scripturam directe & expresse rejici possint, atque ad hoc exigantur Scripturae testimonia. Sed quemadmodum veris fidei principiis immediate credimus, per illuminationem & persuasionem internam Spiritus sancti, qui homines eo suaviter adducit, non per aliud quoddam fidei principium, sed tantum motivis & notis quibusdam quibus divinitas eorum innotescit: sic ad rejicienda & non admittenda quae falso putantur fidei principia sufficit ut destituantur veris verorum principiorum notis, & in iis notari possint ignorantiae & imbecillitatis humanae vestigia.
english: Scripture's perfection does not require that it prove itself. Neither must every false pretended principle of faith be rejected by direct, express proof-texts.

We believe true faith principles immediately through the Spirit's inward illumination and persuasion. He sweetly draws people to them — not by another faith principle, but by motives and marks that make their divinity known.
So to refuse what are falsely counted as faith principles, it is enough that they lack the true marks of true principles, and that traces of human ignorance and weakness show in them.

source_text: XXII. Ac proinde Scripturae perfectioni nihil obest, si demonstrari per eam non possit hunc aut illum librum, qui falso Canonicus praesumitur, revera Apocryphum esse. Imo, etiamsi omnino steteret de non scriptis traditionibus, ad illas rejiciendas sufficere deberet, quod idoneis argumentis eorum authoritas suaderi & probari non potest sicuti Scripturae divinae. Neque nostrum est probare illas non esse divinas, sed eis qui illas urgent atque tuentur, probandum incumbit illas divinas esse.
english: Scripture's perfection is not hurt if it cannot demonstrate that this or that book, falsely presumed canonical, is really apocryphal.
Even if unwritten traditions were granted for the sake of argument, it should be enough for rejecting them that their authority cannot be shown by fit arguments as divine Scripture's can.
It is not our job to prove they are not divine. Those who press and defend them must prove that they are.

source_text: XXIII. Quod spectat autem ad doctrinam quae ex Scriptura hauritur, & in scholis proponi solet, vel consistit in iis quae in Scriptura sacra reperiuntur diserte & expresse posita, aut saltem quae ex iis per consequentias proximas & evidentes deducuntur: cujus generis ea esse debent, quae tanquam articuli, & capita fidei credenda Christiano populo proponuntur, cum nota haereseos in illos qui contraria docent. Vel in iis quae quidem ex Scriptura recte & sane deducuntur, sed tamen non ita clare, & evidenter, & per consequentias magis subtiles & remotas: quod genus proprie non sunt articuli fidei, sed veritates, aut opiniones tantum Theologicae, quarum contrarium gravius appellari non debet, quam error, non vero nomine haereseos notari. Quemadmodum Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae ea tantum esse de fide statuunt, quae sunt a Conciliis suis perspicue & expresse definita, non vero quaecunque nectendo consequentias de consequentis ex iis sese recte colligere posse putant. Ideoque distinguunt inter fidei dogmata, & Theologorum suorum placita, atque sententias, prioribus haeresin, posterioribus errorem opponentes.
english: Doctrine drawn from Scripture and taught in the schools is of two kinds.

First: what Scripture states expressly, or what follows by nearest, evident consequences. Those should be proposed to the church as articles and heads of faith, with the mark of heresy for those who teach the opposite.

Second: what is rightly and soundly drawn from Scripture, yet not so clearly, and by subtler, more remote consequences. Those are not properly articles of faith, but theological truths or opinions. Their contrary should be called error — not heresy.

Rome's own doctors say only what their councils have clearly and expressly defined is de fide — not whatever they think they can weave by chaining consequence upon consequence. So they distinguish faith dogmas from their theologians' opinions: heresy against the first, error against the second.

source_text: XXIV. Inde vero colligi potest quid sit respondendum adversariis, dum impugnantes sufficientiam, quam Scripturae sacrae tribuimus, objiciunt quaedam in nostris Ecclesiis teneri, & doceri, quae tamen per consequentias tam apertas & necessarias ex Scriptura non deducuntur, ut possint Christiani populi fidem obligare, nisi aliunde divina quadam authoritate fulciantur: ut ex. gr. non esse de novo baptizandos eos qui semel apud haereticos baptismum susceperunt. Etenim dogma istud, & alia nonnulla in Ecclesiis nostris tenentur quidem, & docentur, ut Scripturae consentanea, & praeterea longo usu & communi fidelium suffragio probata, quae propterea temerarium est damnare atque rejicere: nec tamen eam illis tribuimus necessitatem, ut Christianorum fidem necessario obligent, adeo ut qui aliter sentit sit e fidelium numero expungendus, & accensendus haereticis, quibus minime vellemus annumeratum Cyprianum virum sanctum & Christi martyrem, qui de baptismo haereticorum non idem sensit quod Ecclesiae nostrae.
english: So we can answer adversaries who attack the sufficiency we give Scripture. They object that our churches hold and teach some things not drawn from Scripture by consequences open and necessary enough to bind the people's faith unless some other divine authority props them up — for example, that those once baptized among heretics are not to be baptized again.
That teaching, and some others, our churches do hold and teach as agreeing with Scripture, and as confirmed by long use and the common vote of the faithful. It is rash to condemn and reject them.

Yet we do not give them such necessity that they bind Christian faith as such — as if whoever thinks otherwise must be struck from the faithful and counted a heretic. We would never want Cyprian so numbered: a holy man and martyr of Christ, who did not hold the same view of heretics' baptism that our churches hold.

source_text: XXV. Porro, ex iis quae jam exposita sunt, satis manifestum est, quo sensu commendemus Scripturae plenitudinem, & sufficientiam, & inculcemus illam omnia quae sunt ad fidem & salutem necessaria continere. Istam autem perfectionem non tantum tribuimus Scripturae Veteris & Novi Testamenti, prout ab Apostolis, & viris Apostolicis nobis consignata est: sed, ex quo Deo visum est verbum suum scripto tradere, existimamus Scripturam semper continuisse omnia quae Dei populo & Ecclesiae necessaria erant ad Deum rite colendum, & salutem adipiscendam: nec opus fuisse alio recurrere ad hauriendam fidei & salutis doctrinam.
english: From what we have already set out, it is plain enough in what sense we praise Scripture's fullness and sufficiency, and press that it contains everything necessary to faith and salvation.

We do not give that perfection only to Old and New Testament Scripture as the Apostles and apostolic men handed it down to us. From the moment God saw fit to put his word in writing, we hold that Scripture always contained all that God's people and the Church needed to worship him rightly and to reach salvation — and that they did not need to go elsewhere to draw the teaching of faith and salvation.

source_text: XXVI. Neque contra hoc facit quod Scriptura, qualis jam est, non pauca ad salutem necessaria continet, quae desiderantur in quinque libris Mosis, quibus solis constitit aliquandiu Scripturae sacrae corpus. Etenim sciendum est omnibus aetatibus non eadem fuisse ad salutem necessaria. Nam plurima nunc sub novo Testamento ad fidem & religionem necessario pertinent, quae non semper eandem habuerunt necessitatem. Siquidem Deus omnia caelestis sapientiae mysteria non revelavit simul & semel: sed ut loquitur Apostolus Hebr. 1. πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως multis partibus atque multis modis. Atque, ex quo primum doctrina caelestis scripto consignari coepit, paulatim crevit divinae revelationis lumen, donec ultimis temporibus Christus doctrinae caelestis plenitudinem attulit, & totum de nostra salute consilium nobis annunciavit.
english: It does not count against this that Scripture as we now have it holds not a few things needful for salvation that are missing from Moses' five books — which alone made up sacred Scripture for a time.
The same things were not necessary for salvation in every age. Much that now belongs of necessity to faith and religion under the New Testament did not always have that necessity.

God did not unveil all the mysteries of heavenly wisdom at once. As the Apostle says in Hebrews, he spoke πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως — in many parts and in many ways (Hebrews 1:1). From the first consigning of heavenly teaching to writing, the light of divine revelation grew little by little, until in the last times Christ brought the fullness of that teaching and announced to us the whole counsel of our salvation.

source_text: XXVII. Crescente vero doctrinae caelestis claritate, & amplitudine, crevit quoque Scripturarum corpus. Nam prout Deus, juxta varia Ecclesiae suae curricula, aliquid de novo Prophetis & Apostolis revelavit, illud summatim scripto tradiderunt. Unde procedente tempore auctus est Scripturae Canon.
english: As heavenly teaching grew clearer and wider, the body of the Scriptures grew with it.
When God, along the Church's changing courses, revealed something new to the Prophets and Apostles, they put it down in writing in summary. So as time went on, the Canon of Scripture was enlarged.

source_text: XXVIII. Sed quanto plura Deus revelavit, & magis distincte, tanto pleniorem & magis distinctam fidem ab hominibus exegit. Quum vero parcior atque obscurior erat revelatio, ad pauciora quoque fides extendebatur. Nam mensura fidei est divina revelatio: neque ad salutem opus est plura nosse & credere, quam sint ea quae Deus revelavit.
english: The more God revealed, and the more distinctly, the fuller and more distinct faith he required of men.
When revelation was thinner and darker, faith reached fewer things as well. Divine revelation is the measure of faith: for salvation we need not know and believe more than God has revealed.

source_text: XXIX. Itaque quanquam Scriptura, quum primum per Mosen data est, non omnia contineret quae nobis nunc necessaria sunt, sufficienter tamen continebat ea quae tunc populo Israelitico necessaria erant. Eamque perfectionem semper habuit Scriptura divina, ut omnia complecteretur, quae Ecclesiam facere & scire opus erat.
english: So although Scripture, when first given through Moses, did not contain everything now necessary for us, it still sufficiently held what the people of Israel then needed.
Divine Scripture always had that perfection: it took in all the Church needed to do and to know.

source_text: XXX. Id tamen intelligendum videtur cum hac cautione, nempe sublatis viris θεοπνεύστοις per quos crevit divinae revelationis lumen, & editis eorum scriptis. Ut excipiatur tempus quo viva vox eorum in Ecclesia resonabat, nec dum scriptis consignaverant quae Deo placitum erat de novo ipsis revelare. Nam, exempli gratia, quum Apostoli praedicare coeperunt, neque adhuc quicquam scripserant, Scriptura veteris Testamenti non continebat omnia ad salutem necessaria, nisi confuse & implicite, quatenus nos ad verum Messiam remittebat, a quo plenius de Dei voluntate edoceremur.
english: Take that with this caution: once the θεόπνευστοι men through whom revelation's light grew are gone, and their writings are out.

Except the time when their living voice still sounded in the Church, before they had put in writing what God was pleased to reveal to them anew. For example, when the Apostles began to preach and had not yet written anything, Old Testament Scripture did not hold all needful for salvation except in a mixed, implicit way — inasmuch as it sent us to the true Messiah, from whom we would be taught God's will more fully.

source_text: XXXI. Sed postquam terris exempti sunt, & in coelum translati illi, quorum ore & calamo Deo visum est uti ad sua mysteria Ecclesiae tradenda, nihil ad fidem & salutem pertinere existimandum est, quod non reperiatur in scriptis quae reliquerunt, & fidelibus commendárunt, ut in Ecclesia essent fidei norma & regula. Nec eorum doctrina alibi quam in eorum scriptis tuto & certo quaeri & inveniri potest.
english: But after those men were taken from the earth and translated into heaven — whose mouth and pen God was pleased to use to hand his mysteries to the Church — nothing is to be counted as belonging to faith and salvation that is not found in the writings they left and entrusted to the faithful as the Church's norm and rule of faith.
Their teaching cannot be sought or found safely and certainly anywhere but in their writings.

source_text: XXXII. Ultro quidem fatemur Prophetas & Apostolos hominesque alios a Deo inspiratos, plurima viva voce dixisse & docuisse, quae in sacris literis verbatim expressa non reperiuntur. Nec etiam negamus fieri potuisse ut Apostoli & viri θεόπνευστοι in Ecclesia olim multa ordinaverint, circa formam divini cultus, & varias Ecclesiasticae politiae circumstantias, quae non sunt in sacris literis perscripta. Atque etiam historica nonnulla ab iis accepta potuisse apud fideles conservari & transmitti ad posteros.
english: We freely admit that the Prophets and Apostles and other men inspired by God said and taught many things by living voice that are not found set down word for word in sacred Scripture.

Nor do we deny that the Apostles and θεόπνευστοι men may once have ordered many things in the Church about the form of divine worship and various circumstances of church polity that are not written out in Scripture. Some historical items received from them may also have been kept among the faithful and handed on to later ages.

source_text: XXXIII. Verum illud arcte tenemus, summam eorum, quae homines sancti, divino Spiritu acti, docuerunt & prolocuti sunt, quantum ad salutem & fidem sufficit, Scriptura sacra contineri; nec quicquam eos docuisse, quod sit ad religionem alicujus momenti, quod in sacris literis abunde traditum non sit.
english: Yet we hold this tightly: the sum of what holy men, moved by the divine Spirit, taught and spoke — so far as suffices for salvation and faith — is contained in sacred Scripture.
They taught nothing of any weight for religion that has not been handed down abundantly in the sacred letters.

source_text: XXXIV. Praeterea quoque asserimus, ea, quae ab Apostolis instituta fuerunt circa ritus divini cultus, & Ecclesiastici regiminis circumstantias, & de quibus tamen Scripturae sacrae silent, esse potestati Ecclesiae permissa, ut ea, pro temporum & locorum ratione, varie immutare posset, sub hac tantum regula & cautione generali, ut omnia fiant ordine & decenter in Ecclesia Dei.
english: We also assert that what the Apostles instituted about rites of divine worship and circumstances of church government — where sacred Scripture is silent — was left to the Church's power.
She may change those things variously for times and places, under this general rule alone: that all things be done in order and decently in the Church of God (1 Cor. 14:40).

source_text: XXXV. Denique, quod praecipuum est, & unde reliqua sequuntur, illud constanter affirmamus eorum quae Apostoli docuerunt, aut instituerunt, nihil nos pro omnino certo & comperto habere, nisi ea quae sunt tradita & consignata in sacris literis. Et hoc quia post Apostolos, & viros Apostolicos, nulli amplius fuerunt in Ecclesia viri ἀδιάπτωτοι extra omne erroris periculum positi. Adeoque quicquid de dictis & factis Apostolorum, praeter scripta Canonica, ad nos usque pervenit, non habemus nisi ex fide hominum infirmorum, qui & falli & fallere potuerunt.
english: The chief point — from which the rest follow — is this: of what the Apostles taught or instituted, we hold nothing as fully certain except what is handed down and set in sacred Scripture.

After the Apostles and apostolic men, the Church had no more ἀδιάπτωτοι men set beyond every danger of error. So whatever of their sayings and deeds reaches us outside the Canonical writings comes only on the credit of weak men, who could both err and deceive.

source_text: XXXVI. Unde patet nullam esse traditionem non scriptam, quae authoritate comparari debeat cum scriptis divinis & Apostolicis: adeoque Scripturam esse unicam fidei regulam, cui alia non possit adjungi quae vim eandem habeat obligandi conscientiam, & fidem obstringendi. Ac proinde, si ipsa sufficiens non esset, neque omnia, quae ad fidem pertinent, contineret, sequeretur Ecclesiam ejusmodi regula sufficienti carere, nec illius saluti sufficienter fuisse provisum.
english: So there is no unwritten tradition that should be matched in authority with the divine and Apostolic writings.

Scripture is the sole rule of faith; nothing else can be joined to it with the same power to bind conscience and constrain faith. If Scripture were not enough and did not hold all that belongs to faith, the Church would lack a sufficient rule, and her salvation would not have been adequately provided for.

source_text: XXXVII. Atque hinc est quod a sacrae Scripturae authoritate negative argumentamur. Quandoquidem enim eorum quae Deus per Prophetas & Apostolos revelavit, nihil omnino certi ad nos pervenit, praeter ea quae ipsi divinitus scripto mandarunt, ut aliquid rejiciamus tanquam ad fidem non pertinens, satis est ut in Scriptura fundamentum non habeat, nec possit ex ea probari & deduci.
english: Hence we argue negatively from Scripture's authority.

Of what God revealed through the Prophets and Apostles, nothing certain has reached us except what they themselves divinely committed to writing. To reject something as not belonging to faith, it is enough that it has no foundation in Scripture and cannot be proved or drawn from it.

source_text: XXXVIII. Itaque non omnino quidem contemnimus, & rejicimus traditiones non scriptas circa res historicas, & Ecclesiarum ritus, ordinem, atque politiam: sed tamen nullas admittimus circa fidei dogmata, & ea quae ad mores pertinent. Neque putamus illa quae Spiritus non judicavit opus esse scripto mandari per suos amanuenses Apostolos & Evangelistas, tanta certitudine a nobis sciri posse, aut eandem authoritatem in Ecclesia habere, ac illa quae scriptis voluit consignari, ut aeternae legis vim in Ecclesia haberent.
english: We do not wholly despise or reject unwritten traditions about historical matters and the Churches' rites, order, and polity.

But we admit none for the dogmas of faith, or for what belongs to morals. What the Spirit did not judge needful to put in writing through his amanuenses the Apostles and Evangelists cannot be known by us with equal certainty, or hold equal authority in the Church, as what he willed to consign in writing to have the force of an eternal law there.

source_text: I. Ex THEISIBUS praecedentibus de Scripturae plenitudine & sufficientia, quam distincte & dilucide a nobis fieri potuit, exposita est nostrarum Ecclesiarum sententia. Ut vero rem totam in pauca contrahamus, huc illa redire videtur, nempe, ex quo Deus verbum suum scriptis consignari voluit, Ecclesiam in libris sacris habuisse omnia quae pro singulis aetatibus, & varia Dei dispensatione ad salutem ita necessaria erant, ut nemo posset citra salutis dispendium contrarium docere, tueri ac tenere: sive quod eodem recidit, Scripturam sacram semper continuisse omnia quae ad corpus & substantiam religionis pertinebant, & ex Dei instituto necessaria erant, quamvis determinatio multarum circumstantiarum quae ad divini cultus, & Ecclesiasticae disciplinae exercitium pertinent, fuerit potestati Ecclesiae permissa, non sigillatim in Scriptura praescripta.
english: From the preceding theses on Scripture's plenitude and sufficiency — as clearly as we could — we have set out our Churches' teaching.

In short: once God willed his word consigned in writing, the Church in the sacred books had all that each age and God's varied dispensation made so needful to salvation that no one could teach, defend, or hold the contrary without loss of salvation.

Or the same point: sacred Scripture has always held all that belongs to the body and substance of religion and is necessary by God's institution — though many circumstances of worship and church discipline were left to the Church's power, not prescribed one by one in Scripture.

source_text: II. Non tamen omnia illa quae necessaria dicimus in Scriptura de verbo ad verbum reperiri, sed, vel verbis aequipollentibus, vel saltem ita ut singula ex Scriptura deduci possint per necessariam atque evidentem consequentiam, citra opem alterius fidei principii, ad quod Scriptura nos remittat, ut ex eo cognitionem uberiorem hauriamus.
english: We do not claim every necessary point stands in Scripture word for word.

It may stand in equivalent words, or at least so that each item can be drawn from Scripture by a necessary and clear consequence — without needing another principle of faith to which Scripture would send us for fuller knowledge.

source_text: III. Ac praeterea fidei principia Scriptura quidem contineri, quoniam sunt ipsa Scriptura, non aliquid extra Scripturam; non quod ex Scriptura sacra probari debeant aut possint. Reliqua vero omnia quae ad religionem & doctrinam sacram pertinent, vel disertis textibus probari, aut ex Scripturis per apertas & proximas consequentias deduci, cujusmodi sunt ea quae proprie dogmata fidei appellari debent: vel solummodo per consequentias remotiores & minus evidentes ex reconditiore Scripturae penu veluti depromi, cujusmodi sunt multae Theologicae veritates in Scholis Orthodoxis proponi & doceri solitae.
english: The principles of faith are contained in Scripture because they are Scripture itself — not something outside it — and not because they must or can be proved from Scripture.

Everything else in religion and sacred doctrine either is proved by express texts, or drawn from Scripture by open, near consequences (what properly count as dogmas of faith), or only fetched by more remote, less plain consequences from Scripture's deeper store (many theological truths taught in the Orthodox schools).

source_text: IV. Quibus addendum est Ecclesias nostras illud arcte tenere, quae ad salutem necessaria sunt, non posse aliunde, quam ex Scriptura peti certo & infallibiliter, nec ullum esse praeter Scripturam Dei verbum, quo confirmari possint ea quae fidei sunt, adeoque Scripturam sacram unicam esse fidei regulam, cui non possit alia adjungi quae sit paris authoritatis.
english: Our Churches also hold tightly: what is necessary to salvation cannot be sought elsewhere than from Scripture — with certainty and without fail.
Besides Scripture there is no word of God by which the things of faith can be confirmed. Sacred Scripture is the sole rule of faith; nothing of equal authority can be joined to it.

source_text: V. Sequitur jam ut exquiramus quae sit de hac quaestione Doctorum Ecclesiae Romanae sententia. Primo igitur docent, Scripturam non esse datam Ecclesiae in hunc finem, ut esset unica fidei regula, atque ut ex ea sola religionis instituta & fidei dogmata peti & erui deberent. Itaque non esse necesse, ut omnia quae pertinent ad fidem atque mores, ex Scriptura sacra probentur. Non negant tamen illa, quae ad salutem singulis simpliciter necessaria sunt, in Scriptura sacra reperiri, ut videre est apud Bellarminum, De verbo Dei lib. 4. cap. 11. §. ultimo. Ubi respondens ad illud Augustini quod a nostris pro sua sententia afferri solet, In his quae aperte posita sunt inquit, Scriptura inveniri illa omnia quae continent fidem moresque vivendi. Limitat, inquit, de illis dogmatibus quae necessaria sunt omnibus simpliciter, qualia sunt quae habentur in Symbolo Apostolico, & in Decalogo. Et in sequentibus probat illud ejusdem Augustini, Credo quod etiam hinc divinorum eloquiorum clarissima authoritas esset, si homo illud sine dispendio promissae salutis ignorare non posset.
english: We turn next to the Roman doctors on this question.

First they teach that Scripture was not given so the Church would have it as the sole rule of faith, or so that religion's institutes and the dogmas of faith would have to be sought from it alone. So not everything that belongs to faith and morals need be proved from sacred Scripture.

They do not deny that what is simply necessary to each person's salvation is found in Scripture — see Bellarmine, De verbo Dei 4.11 (last section). Answering Augustine's line our side cites (In what is openly set down in Scripture are found all things that contain faith and the way of life), he limits it to dogmas simply necessary for all, such as the Apostles' Creed and the Decalogue, and presses Augustine's further point about ignorance that would cost promised salvation.

source_text: VI. Porro etiam totam doctrinam, sive de fide, sive de moribus, necessariam, non quidem singulis simpliciter, sed toti Ecclesiae aliqua ratione Scriptura contineri non negant Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae: sed solum non expresse contineri affirmant, ut videre est apud Bellarminum 4. de Verbo Dei cap. 3. §. 2. Et similiter Stapletonus agens de principiis fidei doctrinalibus, Controv. 5. quaest. 5. art. 1. dum hanc quaestionem explicat, varios modos proponit quibus tota doctrina salutis in Scripturis contineatur. Et primo quidem hunc, quod Scriptura sacra veram Ecclesiam indicans, & ad eam nos mittens, per eam nos omnia necessaria docet. Deinde etiam istum, quod ex multis illis dogmatibus quae in Scripturis aperte posita sunt, reliqua possunt firmiter deduci, sicut dogma de duabus in Jesu Christo naturis ex Filii Dei incarnatione. Nam, inquit, etiam hoc sensu omnia ad fidem necessaria Scripturis comprehendi verum est & Patres docent.
english: Roman doctors do not deny that Scripture contains the whole necessary doctrine of faith or morals — not simply for each person, but somehow for the whole Church. They only deny that it is contained expressly (Bellarmine, De Verbo Dei 4.3 section 2).

Stapleton (Controv. 5 q.5 art.1) offers modes by which the whole saving doctrine is in Scripture: first, Scripture points to the true Church and through that Church teaches all that is needed; second, from dogmas openly set in Scripture the rest can be firmly drawn — as two natures in Christ from the Son's incarnation. Even in that sense, he says, the Fathers teach that all faith needs is comprehended in Scripture.

source_text: VII. Et quamvis in hac quaestione omnes Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae non eodem modo loquantur, sed alii plus, & alii minus Scripturae videantur hac in re tribuere; in eo tamen omnes conveniunt, omnia quae sunt ad aeternam salutem necessario requisita, in Scriptura sacra contineri explicite, vel implicite, expresse vel virtute, & tanquam in semine, si ad eum sensum Scripturae investigantur quem intendit Spiritus sanctus.
english: Roman doctors do not all speak alike here — some seem to grant Scripture more, some less.

Yet they all agree: everything necessarily required for eternal salvation is in sacred Scripture explicitly or implicitly, expressly or by virtue, and as in seed — if Scripture is read in the sense the Holy Spirit intends.

source_text: VIII. Sed negant omnes ea quae ad doctrinam fidei & morum in Ecclesia necessaria sunt in Scripturis ita contineri omnia, ut sufficienter inde peti & hauriri possint, sine ope traditionis, & verbi cujusdam non scripti, quod in Ecclesiae corde depositum est.
english: Yet they all deny that everything the Church needs for the doctrine of faith and morals is so contained in Scripture that it can be sufficiently sought and drawn from there alone.
They still require the help of tradition and of an unwritten word deposited in the Church's heart.

source_text: IX. Etenim Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae communi consensu docent, Christum Dominum nostrum, & Apostolos ejus, multa docuisse & instituisse ad fidem & divinum cultum pertinentia, quae in sacris literis expressa non reperiuntur, nec sufficienter inde possunt erui: adeoque doctrinam Christianam & Apostolicam partim Scriptura, partim verbo quodam non scripto, & ore tenus tradito contineri.
english: Roman doctors agree: Christ and the Apostles taught and set up many points of faith and worship that sacred Scripture neither states expressly nor yields sufficiently when mined alone.
Christian and Apostolic doctrine, on their view, rests partly on Scripture and partly on an unwritten word passed along by mouth.

source_text: X. Istud autem verbum non scriptum Ecclesiarum rectoribus & praepositis commendatum, & eorum fidei commissum, de manu in manum postea traditum fuisse volunt, & perpetua Episcoporum & Pastorum successione sincerum & incorruptum ad nos usque pervenisse.
english: That unwritten word, they say, was placed in the charge of the churches' rectors and overseers.
Hand to hand it was then passed down, and through unbroken succession of bishops and pastors it has reached us pure and unspoiled.

source_text: XI. Atque hae sunt quas vocant traditiones non scriptas, quo nomine intelligunt dogmata & instituta pertinentia ad fidem atque religionem, quae Scripturis canonicis consignata non fuerunt. De quibus, ut quae sit eorum sententia, distinctius intelligatur, sciendum est, fatentibus ipsis Pontificiis, traditionis nomen ex se generale esse, & significare doctrinam omnem quae ab uno traditur & communicatur alteri, sive per scriptum, sive extra Scripturam. Et ita tradere est idem quod docere, & traditio idem quod documentum. Sed tamen usus Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum traditionis vocem plerunque restringit ad doctrinam non scriptam, sed viva voce traditam: & ita sumunt hanc vocem Pontificiae Scholae. Neque tamen per doctrinam non scriptam, intelligunt eam quae nullibi scripta est, sed quae scripta non est a primo authore, seu potius, ut eorum quidam accuratius dicunt, quae scripta non invenitur in libris Canonicis Prophetarum & Apostolorum.
english: What they label unwritten traditions are dogmas and religious institutes never lodged in the canonical books.
Even Pontificians grant that tradition as a word is broad: any teaching one person communicates to another, in writing or outside Scripture. Handing on equals teaching; tradition equals a teaching.
Church writers, however, usually narrow the term to teaching given by living voice rather than writing — and that is how the Pontifician schools use it.
They do not mean a doctrine that exists nowhere in writing, but one the first author never wrote — or, more carefully, one absent from the Canonical books of Prophets and Apostles.

source_text: XII. Porro traditiones varie partiuntur. Sed partitio quae hic maxime consideranda est, illa est quae sumitur ab authoribus ad quos referendae sunt. Dicunt enim traditiones, alias esse Divinas, alias Apostolicas, & alias Ecclesiasticas. Divinas traditiones vocant ea, quae, ut existimant, Christus ipse ἀγράφως docuit & instituit: nec tamen usquam in sacris literis inveniuntur. Hujusmodi traditio ipsis est unctio illa ex oleo & balsamo quae fit in confirmatione, quam inter Sacramenta novae legis numerant. Agnoscunt enim omnia novae legis Sacramenta immediate a Christo institui debuisse.
english: Traditions get many partitions. The one that matters here turns on the authors to whom each kind is traced.
Roman doctors name three: Divine, Apostolic, and Ecclesiastical.
Divine are those Christ himself taught and instituted ἀγράφως (without writing), yet nowhere appear in sacred Scripture.
Their stock case is the oil-and-balsam anointing in confirmation, counted among the new-law Sacraments — for they grant every new-law Sacrament must come immediately from Christ.

source_text: XIII. Apostolicae vero traditiones ab iis proprie dicuntur, quae ab Apostolis praecepta & instituta opinantur, quamvis eorum mentio nulla fiat in scriptis Apostolicis. Ad quas traditiones referunt jejunium quod vocant Quadragesimae, quod ab Apostolis institutum autumant. Et tamen saepe has voces contundunt, traditiones Divinas vocantes ea, quae non Christus ipse, sed Apostoli tantum instituisse putantur: quoniam quae sunt ab iis instituta non sine divini Spiritus afflatu instituerunt. Et vicissim quae ad Christum referunt, traditiones quoque Apostolicas vocant, quoniam eorum quae Christus docuit nihil ad nos pervenit, nisi per Apostolorum scripta & praedicationem. Ecclesiasticae vero traditiones ab iis vocantur quaedam consuetudines antiquae, vel a Praelatis, vel a populis inchoatae, quae paulatim tacito populorum consensu vim legis obtinuerunt.
english: Apostolic traditions, in the proper sense, are commands and institutes they ascribe to the Apostles even when the Apostolic writings are silent.
Under that head they place the Quadragesima (Lent) fast, which they claim the Apostles founded.

Often they blur the labels: what only the Apostles (not Christ) instituted they still call Divine, because those institutes came with the Spirit's breath; and what they tie to Christ they also call Apostolic, since nothing of Christ's teaching reaches us except through Apostolic writing and preaching.
Ecclesiastical traditions are old customs begun by prelates or peoples that, by gradual tacit consent, took on the force of law.

source_text: XIV. Caeterum omnibus istis traditionibus non omnino eandem authoritatem tribuunt. Et quidem traditiones illas quas divinas vocant, eandem vim habere volunt, quam divina praecepta & dogmata quae scripta sunt in Evangeliis. Et similiter traditionibus, quas Apostolicas dicunt, eandem authoritatem tribuendam esse statuunt, quam scriptis Apostolicis. Sed traditionibus Ecclesiasticis minorem aliquanto authoritatem deferunt, eam scilicet, quam habent Canones & Leges Ecclesiae scriptae.
english: Authority is not equal across these kinds.
What they call Divine is given the same force as precepts and dogmas written in the Gospels.
What they call Apostolic is ranked with the Apostolic writings themselves.
Ecclesiastical traditions sit lower — on a level with the Church's written canons and laws.

source_text: XV. Itaque ad duo tantum priora traditionum genera restringunt Decretum Concilii Tridentini, quod habetur Sessione quarta: ubi praecipitur ut traditiones non scriptae pari pietatis affectu suscipiantur atque ipsi libri Scripturae Canonicae. Verba Concilii sunt, Synodus perspiciens Evangelii veritatem & disciplinam contineri in libris scriptis, & sine scripto traditionibus, quae ipsius Christi ore ab Apostolis acceptae, aut ab ipsis Apostolis Spiritu sancto dictante, quasi per manus traditae, ad nos usque pervenerunt, Orthodoxorum Patrum exempla secuta, omnes libros tam Veteris quam Novi Testamenti, cum utriusque unus Deus sit author, necnon traditiones ipsas tum ad fidem, tum ad mores pertinentes, tanquam, vel ore tenus a Christo, vel a Spiritu sancto dictatas, & continua successione in Ecclesia Catholica conservatas, pari pietatis affectu & reverentia suscipit & veneratur.
english: They therefore confine Trent's Session 4 rule — receive unwritten traditions with the same piety as the Canonical books — to the first two kinds alone (Divine and Apostolic).

The Council says: seeing Gospel truth and discipline live in written books and in unwritten traditions received from Christ's mouth by the Apostles, or passed from the Apostles under the Spirit's dictation as if by hand down to us, the Synod, following the orthodox Fathers, receives and venerates with equal piety and reverence every Old and New Testament book (one God their author) and those faith-and-morals traditions spoken by Christ or the Spirit and kept by continual succession in the Catholic Church.

source_text: XVI. Porro Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae plures tradunt regulas, quibus traditiones revera divinae & Apostolicae discerni possint ab aliis, quae falso possent pro talibus obtrudi. Quae tamen omnes regulae ad tres reduci possunt. Prima est quod quicquid Ecclesia Romana tanquam de fide credit, nec tamen in Scriptura clare traditum reperitur, hoc ipso censendum est traditionem esse divinam, seu Apostolicam. Idque nititur duobus quae supponunt fundamentis. Unum est quod Ecclesia Romana errare non possit: Alterum quod tamen Ecclesia illa hodie non regitur novis revelationibus: sed quicquid novit in rebus fidei id totum ab Apostolis & Prophetis didicit.
english: Roman doctors offer several tests for sorting true Divine and Apostolic traditions from fakes; they boil down to three.

First: whatever Rome believes as de fide, yet is not clearly in Scripture, must itself be a Divine or Apostolic tradition — because Rome cannot err, and because she is not ruled by fresh revelation but only by what she learned from Apostles and Prophets.

source_text: XVII. Secunda regula nitens iisdem fundamentis haec est, Quod ea quae servat Ecclesia Romana quae sunt ejusmodi, ut nemo nisi Deus legitime potuerit illa instituere, nec tamen in Scripturis reperiuntur a Deo instituta, ab Apostolis tradita fuisse necesse sit.
english: Second rule, on the same two foundations: what Rome keeps that only God could lawfully institute, yet Scripture never shows God instituting, must have come from the Apostles.

source_text: XVIII. Tertia denique regula eorum est, Quod illud, quod Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae communi consensu docent, ex Apostolica traditione descendere revera pro traditione Apostolica habendum sit: licet tale sit ut ab Ecclesia potuerit institui. Cujusmodi traditionem volunt esse jejunium illud quod vocant Quadragesimale.
english: Third rule: whatever Roman doctors by common consent say descends from Apostolic tradition is to be treated as Apostolic — even when the Church herself could have set it up.
They class the Quadragesimal (Lenten) fast under this head.

source_text: XIX. Sed rursus hae tres regulae in unicam contrahi possunt, hanc nempe, Quod quicquid Ecclesia Romana tanquam divinam aut Apostolicam traditionem proponit, pro traditione tali indubitato sit habendum. Quemadmodum enim Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae authoritatem librorum diu notorum quoad nos ab Ecclesiae praesentis testimonio suspendunt, ita quoque nonnisi ejusdem judicio traditiones veras a falsis certo & infallibiliter discerni & distingui volunt.
english: The three rules fold into one: whatever Rome proposes as Divine or Apostolic tradition must be taken as such without doubt.

As they hang the authority of long-known books on the present Church's witness, so they will have true traditions sorted from false ones only by that same judgment — and that with certainty and infallibility.

source_text: XX. Porro ex iis quae dicta sunt, facile colligi potest quatenus Ecclesiae nostrae cum Ecclesia Romana in hac quaestione conveniant, & quatenus ab ea dissentiant: adeoque quis sit hujus controversiae status. Et primo quidem Ecclesiae Romanae concedimus singula quae pertinent ad Ecclesiae politiam, publicique & externi cultus ceremonias, ex Scriptura peti non posse, sed esse potestati Ecclesiae permissa, & relicta prudentiae praepositorum Ecclesiae.
english: From the foregoing, the controversy's state is clear: where Reformed churches agree with Rome, and where they do not.
First concession: polity and public external-worship ceremonies need not be fetched from Scripture; they are left to Church power and her overseers' prudence.

source_text: XXI. Ultro quoque fatemur illa ipsa quae pertinent ad substantiam & corpus fidei & religionis in Scriptura non contineri verbatim & expresse, sive immediate, sed multa fidei dogmata solummodo ex Scriptura per bonam & legitimam consequentiam deduci.
english: Further concession: the substance and body of faith and religion are not always in Scripture verbatim, expressly, or immediately.
Many faith dogmas come only by good and lawful consequence from Scripture.

source_text: XXII. Vicissim vero Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae nobis concedunt, omnia quae sunt omnibus simpliciter ad salutem necessaria, & quorum fides explicita a fidelibus singulis exigitur, in Scriptura clare & aperte haberi. Ac praeterea nobis largiuntur omnia quae necessaria sunt ad doctrinam fidei & morum in Scriptura saltem virtute & implicite contineri, & ex ea posse per bonam consequentiam deduci.
english: Rome concedes in turn: whatever is simply necessary for every person's salvation, and whose explicit faith each believer must hold, stands clear and open in Scripture.
They also grant that whatever is needed for faith-and-morals doctrine is at least in Scripture virtually and implicitly, and can be drawn by good consequence.

source_text: XXIII. Sed discrimen in eo est, quod omnia quae ad fidem & religionem necessaria sunt, contendimus ex Scriptura ita peti & probari posse, ut opus non sit alio fidei principio, ad quod Scriptura nos remittat plenius erudiendos. Nec etiam ullum fidei principium & regulam extra Scripturam agnoscimus. Doctores vero Ecclesiae Romanae omnia fidei dogmata, & religionis instituta ex Scriptura sufficienter probari non posse contendunt, nisi interveniente Ecclesiae doctrina atque traditione, quam tanquam alteram verbi divini partem paris cum Scriptura sacra authoritatis suscipiendum esse docent.
english: The real split: Reformed hold that everything needed for faith and religion can be drawn and proved from Scripture alone — no second faith-principle to which Scripture remits us for fuller teaching, and no rule of faith outside Scripture.

Roman doctors deny that faith dogmas and religion's institutes can be proved sufficiently from Scripture without intervening Church doctrine and tradition, which they take as another part of the divine word equal in authority with sacred Scripture.

source_text: XXIV. Adeoque tota haec quaestio in duobus versatur. Unum est, an Apostoli quaedam necessaria docuerint aut instituerint, quae non sint sufficienter in sacris literis contenta. Alterum, an Apostolorum documenta & instituta aliunde certo & infallibiliter peti & haberi possint, quam ex Scriptura sacra, nempe ex traditione Doctorum Ecclesiae qui Apostolos secuti sunt, cui par obsequium fidei debeatur atque ipsi Scripturae sacrae. Utrumque affirmant Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae: Theologi vero omnes Orthodoxi utrumque negant.
english: The whole question therefore turns on two points.
First: Did the Apostles teach or institute necessary things not sufficiently contained in sacred Scripture?

Second: Can apostolic teaching and institutes be had with certainty and infallibility from somewhere other than Scripture — namely from the tradition of post-apostolic Church doctors, owed equal faith-obedience with Scripture itself?
Rome affirms both. All Orthodox (Reformed) theologians deny both.

source_text: XXV. Duo igitur affirmamus. Et primo quidem omnia quae pertinent ad substantiam fidei & religionis plene & sufficienter in Scriptura sacra contineri. Deinde, praeter Scripturam non extare ullum Dei verbum quod fidei nostrae sit principium & regula, adeoque nullas traditiones non scriptas aequalis esse cum sacra Scriptura authoritatis. Minime vero istud honoris tribuendum esse traditionibus illis quas Ecclesia Romana tanquam Apostolicas & divinas commendat. Prius autem illud sequitur ex posteriori. Etenim si nullum sit praeter Scripturam Dei verbum, necesse est illam omnia ad fidem & salutem necessaria continere, vel nos jam aliquibus necessariis carere. Et quod inde sequitur, nullam certam ad salutem nobis superesse viam. Itaque omissis iis testimoniis quibus Scriptura suam ipsius plenitudinem & perfectionem commendat, illud praecipue probare contendemus nullum esse Dei verbum viva voce tantum traditum quod cum Scriptura sacra certa sit fidei regula.
english: Two affirmations follow.
First: everything belonging to the substance of faith and religion is fully and sufficiently in sacred Scripture.

Second: besides Scripture there is no word of God that is our faith's principle and rule — so no unwritten traditions equal Scripture's authority, and least of all Rome's so-called Apostolic and divine traditions.

The first follows from the second: if there is no divine word outside Scripture, Scripture must hold all that faith and salvation require, or we already lack necessities and have no sure path of salvation.
So, without rehearsing Scripture's own fullness-texts, the main proof target is this: no living-voice-only word of God stands as a certain faith-rule alongside Scripture.

source_text: XXVI. Primum ergo sic argumentamur. In Ecclesia Judaica, cum Scriptura sacra constaret solis Veteris Testamenti libris, tota salutis doctrina Scriptura continebatur, neque extabant ullae traditiones non scriptae aequalis cum Scriptura sacra authoritatis. Atqui multo magis credendum est totam salutis doctrinam hodie sacra Scriptura contineri, cum Scriptura jam aucta sit Novi Testamenti libris, in quibus exponitur doctrina Christi & Apostolorum. In Ecclesia vero Judaica non extitisse ullas traditiones non scriptas, ejusdem cum Scriptura sacra authoritatis, ex eo colligitur, quod, si quae tales habendae fuissent, proculdubio forent illae quas Judaeorum magistri commendabant, & quarum apud populum observationem urgebant. Sed illas vanas fuisse & hominum commenta docet Christus apud Matthaeum cap. 15. & apud Marcum cap. 7. Quum enim Scribae atque Pharisaei, qui tum erant Ecclesiae Judaicae Doctores, discipulos Christi arguerent, dicentes, Quare discipuli tui transgrediuntur traditionem seniorum? Non enim lavant manus quam panem edunt. Christus vicissim illos increpat, dicens, Quare & vos transgredimini praeceptum Dei per traditionem vestram? Item, irritum fecistis praeceptum Dei per vestram traditionem. Neque solum arguit eorum hypocrisin, quod mandatorum humanorum observationem urgerent, dum ipsi Dei mandata negligebant, & dogmatibus pravis corrumpebant: sed in genere declarat traditiones eorum tanquam frustraneas rejiciendas esse, nec ullas traditiones ut veras & legitimas a falsis & spuriis distinguit. Bene, inquit, de vobis prophetavit Isaias, sicut scriptum est, Populus iste labiis me honorat, cor autem eorum procul abest a me. Frustra vero me colunt docentes doctrinas quae sunt praecepta hominum. Nam omisso Dei praecepto tenetis traditiones hominum, lotiones sextariorum, & poculorum, aliaque similia hujusmodi multa facitis. Ideoque Paulus Coloss. 2. fideles monet ut sibi caveant ab hominum traditionibus, Videte, inquit, Ne quis vos decipiat per Philosophiam & inanem fallaciam, secundum traditionem hominum. Et Galat. 1. sibi ipsi vitio vertit quod ante suam ad Christum conversionem, Supra modum zelator fuerit paternarum traditionum. Cum ergo Christus & Apostoli damnent, ac pro doctrinis hominum habeant Judaeorum traditiones extra Scripturam sacram, pari ratione sequitur rejiciendas & damnandas esse traditiones Pontificiorum: cum illae non majori authoritate nobis commendentur quam Judaeorum olim traditiones.
english: First argument: when Jewish Scripture was only the Old Testament, the whole salvation-doctrine was in Scripture, with no unwritten traditions equal to it.
A fortiori today: Scripture now includes the New Testament books that set out Christ's and the Apostles' teaching, so all the more must salvation-doctrine be contained in Scripture.

That Judaism had no equal-authority unwritten traditions follows because any such would have been the very traditions the Jewish teachers pressed — yet Christ shows those empty human inventions (Matthew 15; Mark 7).

When scribes and Pharisees (then the Jewish Church's doctors) charged the disciples with breaking the elders' tradition by unwashed hands (Matthew 15:2; Mark 7:5), Christ answered that they break God's commandment by their tradition and make God's word void (Matthew 15:3, 6; Mark 7:8-13).

He does not merely rebuke hypocrisy; He rejects their traditions as vain in general and draws no line between true and false extra-Scriptural traditions — citing Isaiah: This people honors Me with lips while the heart is far; in vain they worship Me, teaching human commandments (Isaiah 29:13 via Matthew 15:8-9; Mark 7:6-7).
Paul likewise warns against human tradition (Colossians 2:8) and recalls his own former zeal for ancestral traditions (Galatians 1:14).
So if Christ and the Apostles treat Jewish extra-Scriptural traditions as human doctrines, Rome's traditions fall the same way — they come with no greater authority.

source_text: XXVII. Respondunt adversarii, Christum & Apostolos non reprehendere traditiones, quas Judaei acceperant a Mose & Prophetis, sed traditiones acceptas a quibusdam recentioribus, quae quidem traditiones partim inanes erant, partim cum Scripturis repugnabant: Sed aliam esse rationem traditionum Ecclesiae Romanae, quas illi scilicet a Christo & Apostolis acceperunt. Sed contra sciendum est, traditiones illas, quas Christus exagitat ut doctrinas hominum, pro traditionibus Mosaicis & Propheticis fuisse venditatas. Nam Judaeorum Rabbini, in eo majorum suorum vestigiis insistentes, traditiones suas vocant thorah shebbal peh, quasi dicas, legem oralem, nempe quia volunt illas ore tenus a Mose acceptas, qui illas in monte Sinai ab ipso Deo habuerit, non minus quam legem scriptam, cui proinde volunt illas authoritate pares esse. Jam autem Christi tempore Judaeorum Doctores erant Ecclesiae Doctores & Magistri: siquidem nulla tum erat vera Dei Ecclesia nisi apud Judaeos. Cum ergo nihilominus Christus aperte rejiciat, & pro doctrinis hominum habeat traditiones quas extra Scripturam proferebant, licet ab antiquis illas accepissent, adeoque ab ipso Mose traditas gloriarentur, quam fidem facient hodierni Pontificiorum Doctores traditiones illas, quas se ab ipso Christo & Apostolis ejus per manus patrum suorum accepisse se jactant, revera esse instituta Christi & Apostolorum, non vero humana inventa? Et certe cum inde pateat Ecclesiae magistros in eo posse falli, & pro divinis obtrudere dogmata & praecepta quae mere humana sunt, Inde quoque sequitur nullum extra Scripturam sacram certum Dei verbum reperiri. Etenim, si quod tale verbum Dei exstaret, ab Ecclesiae praepositis accipiendum esset, nec majori authoritate nobis commendaretur.
english: Rome replies: Christ condemned only later, empty, or Scripture-contradicting Jewish traditions — not Mosaic/Prophetic ones — and Rome's traditions come from Christ and the Apostles.

Counter: the traditions Christ attacks as human doctrines were sold as Mosaic and Prophetic. Rabbis call them thorah shebbal peh (oral law), claiming Moses received them viva voce on Sinai equal in authority with the written law.
In Christ's day those Jewish doctors were the Church's only teachers — there was no true Church of God except among the Jews.

Yet Christ still rejects their extra-Scriptural traditions as human doctrines despite ancient/Mosaic pedigree. So why trust today's Roman doctors when they claim hand-to-hand receipt from Christ and the Apostles?

Church teachers can err and push merely human dogmas as divine; therefore no certain word of God stands outside sacred Scripture — for any such word would still have to come through fallible overseers, with no greater warrant.

source_text: XXVIII. Denique quod tradunt & docent Ecclesiae Doctores non potest rejici tanquam humana traditio, nisi quia est extra Scripturam. Etenim, si Dei verbum Scriptura sacra determinatum non esset, sed praeterea extaret verbum Dei non scriptum, jure possent obtendere Ecclesiae Doctores sua documenta esse illud ipsum Dei verbum. Et revera, si ad aliquod verbum Dei non scriptum nobis recurrendum esset, unde potius deberet accipi quam ab ipsis? Cum ergo nihilominus contingat, teste Christo, Ecclesiae Doctores pro Dei verbo proponere quod non est aliud quam humanum commentum; inde manifestum est habendum esse pro doctrina hominum, quicquid extra Scripturae substantiam proponi potest, & Scripturam regulam esse ad quam omnia examinanda sunt: alioquin, ut diximus, Magistrorum Ecclesiae praecepta & documenta, tanquam traditiones humanae, rejici non possent.
english: Church teachers' delivery can be rejected as human tradition only because it stands outside Scripture.

If God's word were not bounded by Scripture and an unwritten divine word also existed, teachers could rightly claim their teaching is that word — and if we needed an unwritten word, where else would we take it?
Yet Christ shows Church doctors can propose mere human invention as God's word.

Therefore whatever can be proposed outside Scripture's substance counts as human doctrine, and Scripture is the rule for examining all things — otherwise magisterial precepts could never be rejected as human traditions.

source_text: XXIX. Praeterea valde notandum est quod in sua responsione adversarii concedunt, nempe Christum ibi reprehendere traditiones quasdam a quibusdam Mose & Prophetis recentioribus acceptas. Etenim inde sequitur pari saltem jure damnandas, & rejiciendas esse traditiones illas quas Pontificii Ecclesiasticas vocant, id est, multa quibus putatur Deus coli, & quae tamen nec Christus, nec Apostoli ejus instituerunt, sed Pastores & Doctores posteriorum saeculorum: quae certe traditiones magnam partem constituunt institutorum Ecclesiae Romanae. Nam traditiones illae non sunt minus mandata & praecepta hominum quam quae olim a senioribus Judaeorum instituta erant. Ideoque non minus in illas congruunt Isaiae verba a Christo prolata, atque confirmata, Frustra colunt me docentes doctrinas & mandata hominum.
english: Note Rome's own concession: Christ rebuked traditions from teachers later than Moses and the Prophets.

By the same right, so-called Ecclesiastical traditions fall — rites and worship practices invented by later pastors and doctors, not by Christ or the Apostles — and those make up much of Rome's system.
They are no less human commandments than the Jewish elders' once were.
Isaiah's words, cited and confirmed by Christ, fit them equally: In vain they worship Me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men (Isaiah 29:13; Matthew 15:9; Mark 7:7).

source_text: XXX. Ad illud vero quod dicunt adversarii Judaeorum traditiones fuisse sacrae Scripturae contrarias, suas vero non item: observandum est multas Judaeorum traditiones non fuisse directe, & sua natura legi divinae contrarias, sed tantum quatenus erant legis additamenta, cum lex divina quicquam sibi addi prohibeat. Ita mos ille abluendi manus religione quadam ante cibi sumptionem ex se nihil mali habere videtur, nec quod sit directe Scripturae contrarium. Et tamen haec est illa ipsa traditio quam speciatim carpit Christus. Quod si dicant Pontificii saltem inanem esse, verum quidem illi dicent. At non minus quadrat in illorum traditiones. Nec enim minus inanes & vanae sunt. Quod si res ex humanae rationis judicio aestimetur, mos ille Judaeorum comperietur non minorem sapientiae speciem habere, quam Pontificiorum pleraque instituta. Sed Christus non damnat simpliciter Judaeorum traditiones, vel quia inanes erant, vel quia erant Scripturae contrariae; sed praeterea in genere, quoniam erant mandata & doctrinae hominum. Quod de traditionibus Pontificiorum non minus verum est.
english: Rome says Jewish traditions contradicted Scripture, but theirs do not.
Many Jewish traditions were not evil or directly anti-Scripture by nature — only unlawful as additions, since divine law forbids adding to itself.
Hand-washing before meals looks harmless and not directly against Scripture — yet that is the very tradition Christ specially targets.
Calling it empty helps Rome nothing: their traditions are no less empty, and by mere human wisdom Jewish washings look no less wise than most Roman institutes.
Christ's verdict is broader: He damns them not only as empty or contrary, but in general as human commandments and doctrines — and that charge fits Rome's traditions equally.

source_text: XXXI. Adde quod de plerisque Pontificiorum traditionibus probare facile est illas non tantum esse praeter Scripturam, & Scripturae additas, quod ipsum aliquatenus Scripturae contrariatur, sed etiam directe cum Scriptura pugnare. Nam, verbi causa, juxta Ecclesiae Romanae traditionem, & licet, & expedit Eucharistiae sacramentum sub sola specie panis fidelibus administrare. Et tamen Christus in Evangelio hoc sacramentum instituens expresse dixit de calice, Bibite ex hoc omnes. Similiter Deus in secundo Decalogi praecepto vetat ullam imaginem religiose coli. Et multis in locis speciatim prohibet, ne quis aliquam Dei similitudinem effingere praesumat. Sed traditio Ecclesiae Romanae docet licitum & utile esse Dei & Angelorum, hominumque morte functorum imagines in templis collocare, & coram iis procumbere, illasque venerari & religiosis ritibus colere. Denique eadem traditio perhibet Christum in Missa quotidie offerri in verum & proprie dictum sacrificium, quamvis in ea nihil patiatur. Epistola vero Pauli ad Hebraeos praedicat unicam tantum esse Christi oblationem, & Christum sese saepius non offerre, quia pati saepius non potest. Unde manifestum redditur traditiones quas Ecclesia Romana ut Apostolicas & divinas commendat non esse Dei verbum & certam fidei regulam. Nam verbum Dei sibi ipsi contrarium esse non potest. Adeoque quod est contrarium Scripturae, quae sine controversia ab omnibus Christianis ut Dei verbum suscipitur, Dei verbum haberi non debet.
english: Most Roman traditions are not only beside Scripture (already a kind of conflict as unlawful additions) but often fight Scripture directly.

Example — communion in one kind: Rome says it is lawful and expedient to give the Eucharist under bread alone; yet Christ instituting the sacrament said of the cup, Drink from this, all of you (Matthew 26:27).

Example — images: the second commandment forbids religious worship of any image, and Scripture often forbids fashioning a likeness of God; Rome teaches placing and religiously venerating images of God, angels, and the dead in churches.

Example — the Mass: Rome holds Christ is offered daily as a true and proper sacrifice though He suffers nothing there; Hebrews teaches Christ's offering is once for all and He does not offer Himself repeatedly, because He cannot suffer repeatedly (Hebrews 9:25-28; 10:10-14).

Therefore Rome's supposedly Apostolic and divine traditions are not God's word or a certain faith-rule: God's word cannot contradict itself, and what contradicts undisputed Scripture must not be held as God's word.

source_text: XXXII. Praeterea solam Scripturam esse certam fidei regulam, traditiones vero quae extra illam proponuntur dubias & incertas esse, inde patet quod si qua pars doctrinae Christianae ab Apostolis solum viva voce tradita, & memoriae hominum commissa, non vero etiam scriptis mandata esset, certe vel illa ad nos non pervenisset, vel saltem non sine multis corruptelis & depravationibus; adeo ut vix purum ab impuro, germanaque ac sincera veritas ab humanis figmentis & commentis addititiis discerni & secerni posset. Tanta est enim hominum perversitas, ignorantia & negligentia, ut quae simpliciter eorum curae & memoriae commissa sunt, oblivioni facile mandentur, & penitus obliterentur, aut saltem variis modis corrumpantur & adulterentur. Ideoque Scripturae usus plane necessarius est ad certam & accuratam rerum memoriam servandam. Quae vero scriptis consignata non sunt, brevi ex hominum memoria delentur, aut fabulis ita implicantur ut verum a falso distingui non possit. Quod multis experienciis manifestum reddi posset. Nam placita Philosophorum, & instituta Rerumpublicarum quae literis tradita non sunt, sed tantum hominum memoriae commissa penitus interierunt, neque de iis quicquam amplius scitur, nisi si quid forte obiter ab aliquo literis mandatum est. Denique de omnibus illis quae praeteritis temporibus sive gesta, sive dicta sunt, nihil certi habemus praeter ea quae libris tanquam fidis custodibus data sunt asservanda. Si autem Scripturae usus ullibi necessarius est, certe praesertim in iis quae ad religionem & cultum divinum pertinent, circa quae homines natura maxime obliviosi sunt, & ad mentiendum & confingendum proni. Atque in hujus rei fidem Pontificios rogare possumus, ubi nunc sint illae Judaeorum traditiones quas volunt illos a Mose & Prophetis accepisse. Certe ne ipsi quidem Pontificii explicare audent, aut possunt quid traditionibus illis continebatur. Neque de Judaeorum religione & cultu quicquam certi hodie habemus aliunde quam ex Mosis & Prophetarum scriptis.
english: Scripture alone is a certain rule of faith; traditions proposed outside it are doubtful and uncertain.

If any part of Christian doctrine had been left by the Apostles only viva voce, committed to memory and never written, it either would not have reached us, or would have reached us thick with corruptions — so that pure truth could hardly be separated from human inventions.
Men's perversity, ignorance, and negligence easily bury, erase, or adulterate what is trusted only to care and memory. Writing is needed for a sure and accurate record.
What is not written soon vanishes from memory or is tangled in fables until true and false cannot be told apart.

Philosophers' opinions and commonwealth institutes left only to memory have perished, except scraps someone happened to write. Of past deeds and sayings we have nothing certain except what books kept as faithful custodians.
If writing is needed anywhere, it is needed most in religion and worship — where people are by nature forgetful and quick to invent.

Ask Rome where the Jews' alleged Mosaic and prophetic oral traditions are now: even Rome cannot say what they contained. Of Jewish religion and worship we know nothing certain except from Moses and the Prophets in writing.

source_text: XXXIII. At, inquiunt, adversarii, a mundi creatione ad Mosen usque doctrina coelestis per solam traditionem sine scripto conservata est. Cur non ergo similiter Apostolicae traditiones ab Apostolorum temporibus ad nostra usque tempora per mille & sexcentos annos servari potuerint? Sed ad istud dico ante Mosen quidem doctrinam sacram sine scripto aliquandiu servatam fuisse. Verum intra paucos admodum. Nam apud plurimos statim corrupta est, & absurdissimis fabulis involuta: ita ut Dei foedus, & doctrina salutis, in una fere Abrahami familia remanserit, reliquum vero totum genus humanum ad idololatriam & commentitios cultus deflexerit. Adde quod tunc temporis defectum Scripturae supplebant frequentes Dei apparitiones, & familiaria cum Patriarchis colloquia, quibus doctrinam viva voce traditam apud ipsos saepius instauravit & renovavit, eamque non tam incorrupte a piis etiam servatam ad puritatem suam & integritatem revocavit. Sed divinae istae apparitiones, & extraordinaria Dei cum hominibus colloquia, in Ecclesia pridem locum non habent.
english: Rome replies: from creation to Moses, heavenly doctrine was kept by oral tradition alone — so why not apostolic traditions for sixteen hundred years?
Answer: before Moses sacred teaching did survive unwritten for a while — but only among very few.

Among most it was soon corrupted and wrapped in absurd fables; God's covenant and saving doctrine nearly remained in Abraham's family alone while the rest of humankind turned to idolatry and invented cults.

What Scripture later supplied was then filled by frequent divine appearances and familiar talk with the Patriarchs, by which God repeatedly restored the viva-voce teaching and called it back to purity.
Those extraordinary appearances and conversations have long ceased in the Church.

source_text: XXXIV. Atque, ut adversarios hic magis constringamus, rogamus eos quare Deus tandem voluit legem suam scripto mandari, & reliquum Scripturae sacrae corpus confici. Certe negare non possunt, quin id factum voluerit Deus, tum ut succurreretur humanae infirmitati, tum ut occurreretur fraudibus impiorum: & quin fuerit Dei consilium, doctrinam sacram istis libris contentam, ab hominum oblivione, & corruptelis vindicare, & tutam illam reddere contra aliorum quidem negligentiam, aliorum vero fraudes & imposturas. Quandequidem autem res ita se habet, dicant adversarii cur toti doctrinae sacrae Deus ita consultum noluit; sed unam quidem partem scribi voluit, aliam vero non scriptam remanere. Etenim, an pars illa non scripta minus opportuna est fraudibus diabolicis, & oblivioni minus obnoxia, quam pars illa quae scripto mandata est? Et nonne testatur experientia in toto orbe, ubi defuit Scriptura, mansisse quidem nonnulla vestigia divinae doctrinae a Patribus traditae, sed illa fabulis miserandum in modum contaminata fuisse, ritusque sacrilegos & peregrinos introductos, & in horrendam, ut diximus, idololatriam detortos? Adde quod adversarii inter causas, quibus divinam providentiam uti volunt in traditionibus conservandis, numerant scripta Doctorum hominum, quibus consignatae sint. Si ergo opus fuit traditiones scribi quo facilius conservari possent, cur Deus id factum voluisset potius ab hominibus vulgaribus & errori obnoxiis, quam a Prophetis atque Apostolis, quibus caetera doctrinae salutaris capita scribenda mandavit? Et cur, si ea quae ex traditione peti volunt ejusdem momenti sunt cum iis quae sacra Scriptura continentur, haec tabulis authenticis consignari voluit, ista vero in hominum vulgarium scriptis relinquere?
english: Press harder: why did God finally will His law written, and the rest of sacred Scripture composed?

Rome cannot deny the twin aims — to help human weakness and to block the frauds of the ungodly — and that God's counsel was to rescue the doctrine in those books from oblivion and corruption, and keep it safe against negligence and imposture.
Then why not the same care for the whole of sacred doctrine? Why write one part and leave another equal part unwritten?
Is the unwritten part somehow less open to diabolical fraud and forgetfulness than the written part?
Worldwide experience says otherwise: where Scripture was missing, Father-handed vestiges remained, but ruined by fables, foreign sacrilegious rites, and idolatry.

Rome itself counts later doctors' writings among providence's means of keeping traditions. If traditions needed writing to survive, why leave that writing to fallible common authors instead of Prophets and Apostles — and why seal Scripture on authentic tables while parking equal-weight traditions in ordinary men's books?

source_text: XXXV. Addunt Pontificii traditiones suas conservatas fuisse, & ad nostra tempora integras pervenisse per continuum usum in quo apud populum Christianum fuerunt; quemadmodum, inquiunt, conservantur linguae vulgares, etiamsi nullae quandoque exstent grammaticae propter earum usum continuum in aliqua gente. Sed contra est experientia. Sicut enim homines natura sunt inconstantes & valde mutabiles, ita quaecunque sunt in eorum usu, nisi quid aliud obstet, hoc ipso continue mutantur atque alterantur; licet plerunque sensim & sine sensu. Quod manifestum est ipso exemplo quem illi afferunt. Etenim linguae vulgares perpetuo mutationem aliquam recipiunt, quae post aliquot saecula ita notabilis est ut videantur in aliam dialectum transiisse. Et ita quoque in quolibet populo antiqui mores, & consuetudines ab hodiernis plurimum discrepant, saeculorum lapsu semper rebus humanis mutationem aliquam afferente. Idemque facile animadverti potest in Ecclesia ipsa Christiana. Si quis enim peritus historiae Ecclesiasticae, ob oculos sibi ponat Ecclesiae faciem, qualis erat secundo & tertio post Christum saeculo, prout illam ex istius aevi scriptoribus colligere licet, agnoscet statim Ecclesiam Romanam in ritibus & disciplina hodie multum ab ea distare: nec est qui negare possit istis in rebus magnam factam esse mutationem. Unde magis patet necessitas regulae cujusdam firmae atque stabilis, nec simpliciter pendentis ab hominum memoria & bona fide, ad quam corrigi possint abusus & errores in Ecclesia sensim enascentes: qualis regula est sola Scriptura sacra, minime vero traditio non scripta.
english: Rome adds: their traditions survived intact by continuous use among Christians — like vernacular languages, which endure even without grammars because a people keeps speaking them.
Experience says the opposite. People are inconstant; whatever lives only in use keeps changing, often slowly and unnoticed — unless something else holds it fast.
Their own analogy proves it: vernaculars continually shift until, after centuries, they look like another dialect. Ancient customs diverge from today's for the same reason.
Church history shows the same: set the second- and third-century Church beside Rome's present rites and discipline, and the gap is obvious.

So the Church needs a firm, stable rule that does not hang merely on memory and good faith — a rule by which creeping abuses can be corrected. That rule is sacred Scripture alone, not unwritten tradition.

source_text: XXXVI. Et certe quam immerito traditiones non scriptae authoritate cum Scriptura aequantur, inde manifestum est, quod in Scripturis sacris Christum Dominum hoc & illud docuisse, atque instituisse testantur nobis Scriptores divinitus inspirati, & extra omne erroris periculum positi. Sed de dictis & factis Christi & Apostolorum extra Scripturam sacram nihil ad nos pervenisse potest, nisi ex testimonio eorum hominum, qui primis post Christum saeculis in Ecclesia floruerunt, & Apostolis ac viris Apostolicis successerunt: quales sunt illi quos Patres antiquos hodie nominamus, & quorum monumenta inter Christianos supersunt. At omnes illi fuerunt errori obnoxii, & tales ipsi se fatentur, cupiuntque ut scripta sua ad Scripturae normam exigantur; non vero recipiantur ἀθεωρήτως & sine examine. Imo ipsi Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae non paucos errores & naevos in iis annotarunt: idque non tantum quum aliquis eorum solitarius, ut sic dicam, loquitur, aliis tacentibus, vel contra dicentibus: Sed etiam quum eorum plurimi in idem consentiunt, quod multis exemplis potest fieri manifestum. Sic, ex. gr. plerique patres docuerunt animas sanctorum ante resurrectionem divinae visionis gloria frui non posse, ut notat Sixtus Senensis, Bibliothecae sanctae lib. 6. annotatione 365. ubi prolixe citat in hanc rem testimonia Justini, Tertulliani, Clementis, Origenis, Lactantii, Victorini, Ambrosii, Prudentii, Augustini, Theodoreti, & multorum recentiorum. Ejusdem quoque libri annot. 35. observat Veteres sensisse nullam creaturam esse incorpoream, & dogma istud illis sic placuisse, ut inter Catholicas regulas & synodicas sanctiones receptum fuerit. Annotatione vero 26. adducit multa loca Chrysostomi, Origenis, Athanasii, Hilarii, Ambrosii, Hieronymi, Chromatii Episcopi Aquileiensis, Oecumenii, Euthymii, unde probat illos credidisse omne juramentum esse simpliciter illicitum, & Christianis interdictum. Praeterea error fuit apud antiquissimos Patres valde solennis, Christum in terris olim aliquandiu cum sanctis in carne regnaturum: quod sensisse olim Papiam Episcopum Hierapolitanum, Irenaeum, Apollinarium, Tertullianum, Lactantium, Severum & Victorinum, testis est Hieronymus, lib. de viris illustribus in Papia, & libro undecimo in Prophetam Ezechielem. Neque Hieron. ipse & Augustinus audent sententiam istam aperte damnare, ut agnoscit idem Sixtus lib. 5. annot. 19. Denique in eodem lib. annot. 171. refert testimonia Origenis, Ambrosii, Hilarii, Basilii, Lactantii, Hieronymi, unde liquet illos existimavisse omnes homines qui sunt qui fuerunt & qui futuri sunt, uno Christo excepto, examinandos, probandos, & aliquo modo urendos igne conflagrationis mundanae in die judicii. Cum ergo prisci illi Ecclesiae Doctores ita fuerint errori obnoxii, ut dogma falsum atque erroneum ceu veritatem divinam amplecti potuerint, quomodo Ecclesiae posteriorum saeculorum tam certe esse possunt traditiones illae quas nonnisi ex eorum fide & testimonio didicit, atque illud quod consignatum videt in divinis ipsis libris Prophetarum & Apostolorum? Et annon omnino a recta ratione abhorret illud, quod testantur homines qui fallere & falli potuerunt, debere apud Ecclesiam authoritatem parem obtinere cum eo quod Deus ipse per Apostolos & Prophetas testatur?
english: Unwritten traditions are wrongly leveled with Scripture: Scripture's inspired writers, beyond error's reach, tell us what Christ taught and instituted.
Outside Scripture, sayings and deeds of Christ and the Apostles reach us only through early post-apostolic witnesses — the Fathers whose monuments remain.
Those Fathers were fallible, confessed it, and asked that their writings be measured by Scripture — not received ἀθεωρήτως and without examination.
Roman doctors themselves mark many errors and blemishes in the Fathers — not only in lone opinions, but even where many agree.

Examples Sixtus of Siena collects: most Fathers denied the saints the beatific vision before the resurrection; ancients held no creature incorporeal as a received Catholic rule; many forbade all oaths; chiliast hope of an earthly fleshly reign (Papias, Irenaeus, and others); and a purifying world-fire for all except Christ on judgment day — which even Jerome and Augustine hesitate to condemn outright.

If early doctors could hug false dogma as divine truth, later-age traditions learned only from their witness cannot stand as certain beside what God consigned in the Prophets' and Apostles' books — nor can fallible men's testimony claim equal Church authority with God's own.

source_text: XXXVII. Sed ut clarius appareat, quam fallaces sint traditiones, quae tanquam Apostolicae extra Scripturam proferuntur, hic valde considerandum est, quod, si unquam traditiones illae certitudinem aliquam habuerunt, id maxime locum habere debuit primis Ecclesiae Christianae temporibus, quum recens adhuc erat memoria Apostolorum. At jam primis post Christum saeculis traditiones non scriptae ita incertae & variae erant, ut Doctores Ecclesiae de iis inter se certarent, & multi viri alioqui boni traditionum nomine decepti sint, & multa vana atque falsa tanquam Apostolicas traditiones sint amplexi. Ita testatur Eusebius Historiae Ecclesiasticae lib. 3. cap. ult. Papiam illum Episcopum Hierapolitanum, qui proxime post Apostolos vixit, traditionibus multum tribuisse, & inter alia scripsisse quinque libros de sermonibus Domini ex traditione non scripta, sed illos fabulis refertos fuisse. Sic quoque quum aliquanto post de celebratione Paschatis magna contentione inter Ecclesias Orientis & Occidentis certaretur, An scilicet praecise decima quarta lunae, an vero die Dominica post decimam quartam celebrandum esset: Polycrates, & alii Asiae Episcopi, qui prius illud tuebantur, traditionem Joannis & Philippi obtendebant: Victor vero Romanus, & alii Occidentales asserebant se Petrum & Paulum sequi, ut videre est apud Eusebium hist. Eccles. lib. 5. cap. 23. & seqq. & apud Socratem lib. 5. cap. 22. Ita non pauci ex antiquis existimarunt Apostolos instituisse stata quaedam & certa jejunia, hi quidem uno, illi vero alio modo. Sed Augustinus epist. 86. ad Casulanum, & Socrates lib. 5. cap. 22. negant Apostolos quicquam de jejuniis determinasse; Sed Ecclesiis liberum reliquisse quando & quomodo jejunandum esset. Et quum Augustinus in ista epistola tractet quaestionem illam, An Sabbato jejunandum sit, quod faciebant Romani & pauci Occidentales, traditionem Petri Apostoli obtendentes, reliquae vero Ecclesiae omnes aut negligebant, aut etiam illicitum ducebant, caeterorum Apostolorum, a quibus Evangelii doctrinam acceperant, traditione nitentes, judicat interminabilem esse istam contentionem generantem lites, non finientem quaestiones, adeoque ex non scripta traditione nihil certi haberi posse super jejuniorum ratione & modo. Sic etiam Tertullianus libro de corona militis, & Basilius libro de Spiritu sancto, recensent varias traditiones quas Apostolicas esse volunt, ut ex. gr. nefas esse jejunare diebus Dominicis, & iisdem diebus oportere stantes precari, ut & diebus omnibus a Paschate ad Pentecosten, quod etiam sanxit Nicena Synodus. Et tamen ista posterioribus saeculis observata non fuerunt, & pro traditionibus Apostolicis habita.
english: If unwritten apostolic traditions ever had certainty, it should have been strongest while apostolic memory was still fresh.
